c01.title: Scaling from zero to millions of users
c01.summary: Grow capacity gradually by separating bottlenecks, maintaining redundancy, and measuring system behavior.
c01.objectives.0: Explain the evolution from a single server to a distributed architecture.
c01.objectives.1: Choose caching, replication, queues, and sharding according to the bottleneck.
c01.objectives.2: Assess consistency and recovery costs when adding capacity.
c01.sections.0.title: Single server, request flow, and database separation
c01.sections.0.body: Start with a flow you can explain: DNS translates a domain name into an address, then a browser or mobile application sends HTTP to the web server. The server runs business logic and returns HTML or JSON. Initially, the application and database can share a machine; separate them when CPU, disk, or database connections begin competing for resources. Separation allows each tier's capacity and management to evolve independently. Choose SQL for the relationships and transactions you need; choose document, key-value, column, or graph models according to access patterns, rather than assuming NoSQL is always faster.
c01.sections.1.title: Vertical scaling, horizontal scaling, and load balancing
c01.sections.1.body: Vertical scaling adds CPU or RAM to one machine, making implementation straightforward, but hardware limits and a single point of failure remain. Horizontal scaling adds machines and requires requests to be distributed through a load balancer. Health checks remove unhealthy instances from rotation; healthy instances still need spare capacity to absorb their traffic. Adding web servers does not automatically increase database capacity. Measure throughput, utilization, and high-percentile latency before deciding which tier to expand. The load balancer itself must also be redundantly available so that it does not replace one single point of failure with another.
c01.sections.2.title: Database replication and failure recovery
c01.sections.2.body: In the primary–replica pattern, changes are written to the primary and forwarded to replicas. Reads that tolerate delay can be distributed to replicas so the primary can focus more on writes. Replication adds copies, but asynchronous replicas can lag; a user who has just updated a profile may still see the old value. If a replica fails, move reads to healthy copies while accounting for their capacity. If the primary fails, promotion must select a candidate and prevent the old primary from continuing to accept writes. Backups, recovery, and failover testing remain necessary because application errors can also be replicated.
c01.sections.3.title: Application caching: TTL, invalidation, and eviction
c01.sections.3.body: A cache stores frequently read results to reduce trips to the database. With cache-aside, the application looks up a key in the cache, reads the database on a miss, and then fills the cache. TTL limits data age, while eviction policies such as LRU free memory when capacity is full; they solve different problems. After a write, cache invalidation or updates must account for races with readers. A cache outage can suddenly flood the database, so concurrency protection, gradual warming, and staggered TTLs help. Source data remains in authoritative storage, and freshness requirements determine what is suitable for caching.
c01.sections.4.title: CDNs and static asset delivery
c01.sections.4.body: A CDN places copies of images, stylesheets, and JavaScript near users. The edge serves cache hits; a cache miss fetches an asset from the origin and stores it according to caching rules. Long TTLs reduce origin load but delay the visibility of updates, so versioned or hashed asset names make safe changes easier. Plan invalidation, transfer costs, cache keys, and fallback when the CDN has problems. Origin fallback must be limited because all users may switch simultaneously. Private content needs appropriate caching rules so that one user's response is not shared with another user.
c01.sections.5.title: Stateless web tiers and multiple data centers
c01.sections.5.body: A stateless web tier does not store sessions that can only be read on one instance. Sessions can reside in shared storage or use an appropriate token mechanism, allowing another instance to handle the next request. This makes autoscaling and machine replacement easier. Deployment across multiple data centers reduces network distance and the impact of a location failure. GeoDNS is one routing method, but DNS caching means switching is not instantaneous. Define data synchronization, who may write, and behavior when connectivity between locations breaks. Deployment automation and traffic-switching drills keep configurations consistent across locations.
c01.sections.6.title: Message queues, logging, metrics, and automation
c01.sections.6.body: A producer places work in a queue for a consumer to execute asynchronously, such as processing an image after an upload is accepted. A queue absorbs temporary spikes; its backlog keeps growing if the incoming rate continually exceeds consumer capacity. Durability depends on persistence and replication configuration, not merely on using memory. Consumers need acknowledgements, retries, and idempotency to handle redelivery. Logging helps track errors, metrics show latency, error rate, utilization, and backlog age, and alerts guide the response. Automating testing, deployment, rollback, and scaling shortens the change process while retaining capacity limits and health checks.
c01.sections.7.title: Database scaling and sharding
c01.sections.7.body: When one database is no longer sufficient, sharding divides records according to a shard key, such as user_id. Choose a key that balances both data and traffic while keeping common access on one shard. Replication creates copies; sharding divides data ownership. Growth requires resharding and migration that keep requests able to find records. Consistent hashing reduces placement changes when membership changes, but does not eliminate hot keys belonging to popular users. Those users may need caching or dedicated capacity. Cross-shard joins and transactions become more expensive; denormalization helps reads at the cost of synchronizing data copies.
c01.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Horizontal scaling allows additional instances and redundancy.
c01.tradeoffs.0.cost: Routing, shared state, and distributed operations are more complex.
c01.tradeoffs.0.when: When machine limits or availability targets require multiple instances.
c01.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Replicas add read capacity; sharding divides data and writes.
c01.tradeoffs.1.cost: Replicas introduce lag; sharding complicates joins and migration.
c01.tradeoffs.1.when: Distinguish a read bottleneck from the capacity limit of one primary.
c01.pitfalls.0: The number of registered users is not a direct measure of requests per second.
c01.pitfalls.1: Caching and replication do not guarantee that all reads immediately see the latest write.
c01.pitfalls.2: A queue does not resolve a persistent shortage of consumer capacity.

c01.exercise.prompt: Design a profile service with 10,000 reads/s, 500 updates/s, and photo uploads requiring two seconds of processing. Explain the scaling sequence and the failure of one web server.
c01.exercise.hints.0: Separate photo assets, profile reads, and processing work.
c01.exercise.hints.1: Decide whether users must immediately see their profile updates.
c01.exercise.solution: Place a stateless web tier behind a load balancer and store sessions using a shared mechanism. Use a CDN for photos and a profile cache with invalidation after updates. Direct writes to the primary; use replicas only for reads that accept lag, and direct read-after-write to the primary when necessary. Send photo processing to a queue with idempotent workers; measure backlog before adding workers. When one web server fails, health checks remove it and the remaining instances must have enough capacity to carry the load. Consider sharding after measurements show that the primary or data size has become the limit, rather than merely because the user count has increased.
c04.title: Rate Limiter
c04.summary: Limit traffic with algorithms suited to bursts, quota accuracy, and distributed coordination requirements.
c04.objectives.1: Design rules and atomic counters across multiple instances.
c04.objectives.2: Explain throttling responses and behavior when the limiter fails.
c04.sections.0.title: Requirements, rules, and limiter placement
c04.sections.0.body: A rate limiter controls request volume to protect capacity, reduce costs, and limit abuse. Define the identity being limited: user, API key, IP, endpoint, or a combination. Different rules can apply simultaneously, such as login quotas per account and per IP. A client-side limiter helps the user experience but cannot be authoritative because clients can be modified. Application middleware or an API gateway provides server-side control. Placement should account for added latency, rule consistency, memory use, distributed scale, and whether a dedicated service or integration with the available stack makes more sense.
c04.sections.1.title: Token bucket: average rate and bursts
c04.sections.1.body: A token bucket has capacity B and a refill rate of r tokens per second. A request is allowed if tokens are available, then consumes tokens according to its cost; a full bucket does not store anything beyond B. After a long idle period, a client can send a burst up to that capacity, then becomes limited by refill. For example, B=20 and r=5 allow 20 immediate requests, rather than promising that every one-second window always contains at most five. An implementation can calculate refill lazily from the last recorded time. Choose burst capacity and sustained rate separately, with consistent clocks and state updates.
c04.sections.2.title: Leaky bucket: stable output and a bounded queue
c04.sections.2.body: In the leaky-bucket queue model, requests enter a bounded FIFO and are processed at a fixed rate. This smooths output to a service that is sensitive to spikes. When the queue is full, new requests are rejected; when requests wait in the queue, latency increases even if they are eventually accepted. If 30 requests arrive together and processing runs at ten per second, the last request can wait almost three seconds in this simple model. Set a waiting limit so expired work is not still processed. The term leaky bucket is also used for meter variants, so explain whether the system delays requests or merely decides admission.
c04.sections.3.title: Fixed window counters and boundary problems
c04.sections.3.body: A fixed window counter stores a count per identity and interval, such as 100 requests per calendar minute. Each request increments the counter atomically and is compared with the quota; the next interval starts a new counter. Memory use and logic are simple, but interval boundaries can admit excessive bursts within a rolling range. One hundred requests in the last second of the first minute and another hundred in the first second of the next minute produce 200 requests in two seconds. This algorithm fits contracts that genuinely follow calendar intervals, but requires an additional burst limit if downstream cannot absorb that spike.
c04.sections.4.title: Sliding window log: an accurate rolling limit
c04.sections.4.body: A sliding window log retains timestamps of accepted requests within a time range W. Before deciding on a new request, remove timestamps outside the range, count the remainder, and accept only if the count is still below the limit. This avoids the minute-boundary gap of fixed windows because each decision uses a rolling range. A sorted set can support cleanup and counting, but each request requires its own state, so memory consumption grows with the quota and number of active identities. Define timestamp boundary conventions consistently. Cleanup, checking, and recording must form one atomic decision.
c04.sections.5.title: Sliding window counter: a weighted approximation
c04.sections.5.body: A sliding window counter combines counts from the current and previous intervals. A simple estimate is current + previous × (1 − elapsed/W), where elapsed is the position in the current interval. If the old interval contains 80 requests and one quarter of the new interval has elapsed, its old contribution is estimated as 60. This approach uses little state and smooths spikes, but assumes requests in the old interval were reasonably evenly distributed. If they all arrived near its end, the estimate may be too low; the opposite pattern may make it too high. Choose this algorithm for efficiency when some inaccuracy is acceptable, rather than for a strict rolling contract.
c04.sections.6.title: Architecture, coordination, and race conditions
c04.sections.6.body: The general flow takes a client to middleware, which retrieves rules and state from fast storage and then forwards or rejects the request. Across multiple instances, separate counter reads and writes let two requests both pass even when only one quota unit remains. Use atomic operations or scripts that combine checking and state modification; TTL cleans up inactive identities. Sharding state by identity limits the central storage bottleneck. Limit rule complexity and avoid repeated network access for each rule when operations can be combined. Each instance's local quota must be understood as part of the global quota, rather than a duplicate of the full quota.
c04.sections.7.title: Throttling, failures, multiple regions, and monitoring
c04.sections.7.body: Rejected requests need a clear response, usually HTTP 429, and guidance on when to try again when available. Clients should back off so retries do not amplify spikes. When limiter storage fails, fail-open maintains access but allows excess traffic; fail-closed protects capacity but rejects legitimate requests. Choose according to the endpoint and provide a limited fallback. Regional limiters reduce latency, but eventual synchronization can exceed the global quota. Monitor rejection rate, decision latency, state size, and store errors. Rule changes need versioning and observation so a misconfiguration does not suddenly block all users.
c04.tradeoffs.0.benefit: A token bucket allows bursts; a leaky-bucket queue keeps output stable.
c04.tradeoffs.0.cost: Bursts load downstream; queues add waiting time.
c04.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose according to downstream tolerance for spikes and latency.
c04.tradeoffs.1.benefit: The log provides accurate rolling counts; the counter saves state.
c04.tradeoffs.1.cost: The log uses more memory; the counter is an estimate.
c04.tradeoffs.1.when: Use a log for strict limits and a counter when efficiency matters more.
c04.tradeoffs.2.benefit: A global quota combines usage across all locations.
c04.tradeoffs.2.cost: Coordination adds latency and dependencies between locations.
c04.tradeoffs.2.when: Use a global quota when the contractual limit must apply simultaneously across every region.
c04.pitfalls.0: A fixed-window limit of 100 per minute does not mean a maximum of 100 in every rolling 60 seconds.
c04.pitfalls.1: Shared counters without an atomic decision can still admit excess requests.
c04.pitfalls.2: An application rate limiter alone does not stop every form of volumetric network attack.
c04.references.0.label: Source chapter: Rate Limiter
c04.exercise.prompt: An API receives a burst of 40 requests after being idle, but downstream can sustain only 10 requests/s. Determine policies for an interactive endpoint and batch work.
c04.exercise.hints.0: Separate burst capacity from the sustained rate.
c04.exercise.hints.1: Explain whether requests must be rejected or may wait.
c04.exercise.solution: For an interactive endpoint, use a token bucket with a refill rate of 10/s and burst capacity limited to the spike downstream can actually absorb; capacity 40 is unsafe if downstream lacks headroom. Reject excess requests with a throttling response and backoff. For batch work, a leaky-bucket queue with output of 10/s can accept 40 jobs if queue capacity and deadlines allow roughly four seconds to drain in this model. Store consumption decisions atomically per identity on coordinating limiter instances. Monitor rejections and waiting time; a sustained incoming rate above 10/s requires rejection or additional capacity.
c05.title: Consistent Hashing
c05.summary: Map keys onto a ring so membership changes move only part of the data, then use virtual nodes to balance ownership.
c05.objectives.0: Distinguish modulo hashing from changes in ownership on a ring.
c05.objectives.1: Determine which key ranges move when nodes are added or removed.
c05.objectives.2: Assess the benefits of virtual nodes and their limitations for hot keys.
c05.sections.0.title: The modulo rehashing problem
c05.sections.0.body: The mapping hash(key) % N is easy to implement when the number of servers N is fixed. However, changing N changes the divisor for every key, so many keys point to new servers even if only one server is added or removed. In a distributed cache, this movement triggers cache misses and origin load; in storage, it requires substantial data migration. The problem is the change in the placement function, rather than simply the new server's capacity. Consistent hashing preserves key positions and most node positions so membership changes have a more local impact. Continue measuring data movement, warming time, and capacity during the transition.
c05.sections.1.title: Hash space and the ring
c05.sections.1.body: Imagine the hash output space as a circle: after the maximum value, searching returns to zero. Hash stable node identities and every key into the same space. The space size can follow the chosen hash function; a 160-bit space is only one illustration, not an algorithm requirement. Nodes and keys must use consistent encoding rules and hash versions across all routers. The ring can actually be stored as a sorted list of node positions, so it does not require a physical circular graph structure. Collisions or node renaming must be handled with deterministic rules so every router reaches the same decision.
c05.sections.2.title: Lookup and ownership boundaries
c05.sections.2.body: To find a key's owner, locate the first node at or after the key's hash position while moving clockwise. If there is no larger position, use the first node after wrapping around zero. A node owns the range from its predecessor to its own position, with a clear boundary convention, such as (predecessor, node]. Binary search on the sorted positions provides efficient lookup. A key is not assigned to the geometrically nearest node in either direction; the one-way successor rule determines ownership. All participants must receive appropriate membership versions so requests are not directed to different owners during a change.
c05.sections.3.title: Adding nodes and moving keys
c05.sections.3.body: When a new node is placed between P and S, keys in the range (P, new] move from S to the new node. Keys outside that range retain their owners if existing node positions do not change. With an ideal distribution, adding one node to N nodes moves approximately 1/(N+1) of the keys; the actual amount depends on ring positions and key distribution. If the new node has many virtual nodes, movement occurs across several small ranges. Migration must ensure data is available before routing becomes active, or provide fallback to the old owner so cache warming and reads do not cause a spike in failures.
c05.sections.4.title: Removing nodes and recovering data
c05.sections.4.body: When node X is removed, the range previously owned by X is transferred to the next active successor. Routers can immediately calculate the new owner, but placement calculations do not recreate lost data. A cache can refill from its origin, while durable storage requires replicas, backups, or a transfer protocol. If X has virtual nodes, several physical successors may share its responsibility. Graceful removal allows migration time; sudden failure requires detection and recovery. Avoid overly rapid membership changes caused by temporary disruptions, because flapping can repeatedly trigger movement and warming that consume capacity.
c05.sections.5.title: Virtual nodes and heterogeneous capacity
c05.sections.5.body: One position per server can produce very different ranges because hash placement is not always balanced. Virtual nodes represent one server through many positions, such as hash(server_id, index). A server receives a combination of ranges, so variation in ownership tends to decrease as the number of positions increases, assuming good hash distribution. Larger servers can receive more positions to weight capacity. The costs are more ring metadata and migration work. Virtual nodes improve statistical balance, but do not guarantee equal byte counts, CPU usage, or requests on every server when key sizes and popularity differ.
c05.sections.6.title: Hotspots, benefits, and limits of guarantees
c05.sections.6.body: Consistent hashing reduces remapping and makes adding capacity easier, but balancing key counts is not the same as balancing traffic. One popular key still goes to the same owner even when more virtual nodes are added. Solutions may include layered caches, read replicas, splitting hot keys when semantics allow, or request limiting. A good hash helps key distribution but does not change user access patterns. Minimal movement can also preserve an existing imbalance. Monitor byte ownership, request rate, latency, and headroom on each server; use those results to determine weights or additional rebalancing strategies.
c05.sections.7.title: Real-world applications and ring operations
c05.sections.7.body: Techniques in the consistent-hashing family are used to place data or requests in storage, caching, and routing systems. Strong learning examples include Amazon Dynamo's design and Cassandra's token-based partitioner; the algorithm and replication details of each must be examined separately. Do not equate every algorithm that reduces remapping with a virtual-node ring: alternatives such as rendezvous hashing or lookup tables use different mechanisms. When operating a ring, document the membership source, configuration version, transfer strategy, and replica owners. Test node additions and failures with realistic traffic because minimal movement does not automatically yield uninterrupted failover.
c05.tradeoffs.0.benefit: A ring reduces placement changes when membership changes.
c05.tradeoffs.0.cost: Metadata and ring-change protocols are more complex.
c05.tradeoffs.0.when: When cache or storage members are frequently added and removed.
c05.tradeoffs.1.benefit: More positions usually reduce variation in ownership.
c05.tradeoffs.1.when: Use a count that balances distribution against operational cost.
c05.pitfalls.0: Moving clockwise does not mean choosing the nearest node in either direction.
c05.pitfalls.1: Virtual nodes do not solve a single extremely popular key.
c05.pitfalls.2: Calculating a new owner is not the same as recovering data from a failed node.

c05.references.1.label: Dynamo: Amazon's storage design
c05.exercise.prompt: On a ring from 0–99, node A is at 10, B at 40, and C at 80. Determine the owners of keys 5, 25, 70, and 95; then add D at 60 and explain the impact.
c05.exercise.hints.0: Use the clockwise successor with wrap-around.
c05.exercise.hints.1: Identify D's predecessor and the previous owner of its range.
c05.exercise.solution: The initial owners are A for key 5, B for 25, C for 70, and A for 95 because searching wraps around zero. Node D at 60 takes the range (40,60] from C. All four example keys retain their owners; key 50, as an additional example, changes from C to D. If C then fails, its remaining range (60,80] moves to A, including key 70. The ring only changes routing decisions: durable data must be available from replicas or transfers, while a cache needs warming from its origin. Many virtual nodes spread movement across multiple ranges.
c02.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation
c02.summary: Turn product assumptions into testable traffic, storage, latency, and availability requirements.
c02.objectives.0: Calculate average and peak QPS using consistent units.
c02.objectives.1: Estimate media, cache, and server capacity.
c02.objectives.2: Connect availability targets to a downtime budget.
c02.sections.0.title: Powers of two and data units
c02.sections.0.body: Estimation starts with units rather than large numbers. One byte contains eight bits; KiB, MiB, and GiB use powers of 1024, whereas decimal KB, MB, and GB use powers of 1000. Choose one system and keep it throughout the calculation. Powers of two help estimate address spaces, the number of combinations, and memory capacity. Decimal units are often more practical for disks and bandwidth. State whether a figure represents logical data, compressed data, or physical capacity after replication so the result does not appear more precise than its assumptions.
c02.sections.1.title: The latency hierarchy
c02.sections.1.body: CPU cache, memory, SSD, mechanical disk, and network access operate on very different timescales. The source figures are historical illustrations, not benchmarks for the hardware you will use. Use this hierarchy to identify the dominant decisions: eliminating an inter-region round trip often matters more than saving a few instructions. Caching reduces storage access, batching reduces network trips, and compression trades CPU work for bandwidth. Distinguish the latency of one request from the throughput of many parallel requests; fast operations do not automatically provide unlimited capacity as queues grow.
c02.sections.2.title: Availability and downtime budgets
c02.sections.2.body: Availability is the proportion of time or requests that meet the service definition. In a time-based approach, annual downtime equals 365 days multiplied by one minus availability. A 99.9 percent target allows about 8.76 hours per year, whereas 99.99 percent allows about 52.56 minutes. The success definition, measurement window, and scheduled maintenance must be clear before this figure becomes a commitment. Many components in series can reduce overall availability. Replication helps, but common failures such as configuration mistakes can disable every replica at once.
c02.sections.3.title: Microblog traffic example
c02.sections.3.body: Start with monthly active users, convert them to daily active users, and then multiply by each user’s daily activity. If 300 million monthly users have a 50 percent daily activity ratio and write two posts, there are 300 million posts per day. Dividing by 86,400 gives about 3,472 write operations per second. A peak factor of two gives about 6,944. This is write traffic only; reading feeds, uploading media, and fan-out need separate calculations. Regional patterns and major events can produce a different peak factor.
c02.sections.4.title: Media storage and retention
c02.sections.4.body: Object size and the fraction of posts containing media determine storage more than small metadata fields do. With 300 million posts per day, 10 percent containing media, and an average size of one MB, media grows by about 30 TB per day in decimal units. Five-year retention produces 54.75 PB of logical data before replication, indexes, or backups. Do not assume all media has the same size; use a weighted average of images and videos. Retention, deduplication, compression, and user deletion can change the projection. Separate object storage from the metadata database so each can scale independently.
c02.sections.5.title: Rounding, caching, and server capacity
c02.sections.5.body: A useful estimate explains design decisions with simple numbers. Round to obtain orders of magnitude, write down assumptions, and retain units at every step. Estimate the number of servers by dividing peak QPS by safe throughput per server, then rounding up; safe throughput must leave room for failures and spikes. Estimate cache capacity from the working set rather than necessarily the entire database. Test sensitivity with several scenarios because an incorrect media ratio or user activity assumption often matters more than a small rounding error.
c02.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Rounding makes assumptions and orders of magnitude easy to inspect.
c02.tradeoffs.0.cost: It is insufficient for final capacity purchasing.
c02.tradeoffs.0.when: Use it when choosing architecture; measure before provisioning.
c02.tradeoffs.1.choice: A larger cache versus more frequent storage access
c02.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Keeping the working set in memory reduces read latency.
c02.tradeoffs.1.cost: Memory is expensive and invalidation adds complexity.
c02.tradeoffs.1.when: Choose this when access is concentrated and the hit ratio is measured.
c02.pitfalls.0: Using average QPS as peak capacity.
c02.pitfalls.1: Mixing bit/s and byte/s without a factor of eight.
c02.pitfalls.2: Assuming logical size already includes replicas and backups.
c02.references.0.label: Source chapter
c02.exercise.prompt: Design capacity for a service with 20 million DAU, 3 posts per day, 20% containing 2 MB media, 2-year retention, and 3 replicas. Calculate peak QPS with a peak factor of 4.
c02.exercise.hints.0: Separate posts per day from QPS.
c02.exercise.hints.1: Multiply only the media fraction by media size, then apply retention and replication.
c02.exercise.solution: There are 60 million posts per day: about 694 average QPS and 2,778 peak QPS. Media produces 12 million objects or 24 TB per day. Two years produces 17.52 PB logically; three replicas produce 52.56 PB physically before metadata and backups. Use object storage for media, a database for metadata, and write capacity with headroom. This calculation does not include feed reads or fan-out costs.

c03.title: System design framework
c03.summary: Four steps keep a design discussion focused on requirements, decisions, and capacity evidence.
c03.objectives.0: Turn ambiguous questions into a clear scope.
c03.objectives.1: Explain the initial architecture and use-case flows before a deep dive.
c03.objectives.2: Allocate time to critical components and failure assessment.
c03.sections.0.title: Understand the problem and establish scope
c03.sections.0.body: Design questions are usually deliberately ambiguous. Ask about core features, users, platforms, scale, latency, consistency, and technology constraints before choosing a database. For a news feed, the number of friends, media support, and chronological ordering change fan-out costs and read behavior. Record assumptions openly so the other participant can correct them. The first stage aims to establish a testable design contract rather than collect every possible feature. Distinguish required capabilities from extensions so secondary features do not consume time needed for the main architectural decisions.
c03.sections.1.title: Propose and agree on a high-level design
c03.sections.1.body: Draw the main components and their responsibilities: clients, APIs, storage, caches, queues, and content delivery services where relevant. Explain their relationships through the journey of a request rather than merely naming technologies. For a feed, separate post publication from feed retrieval; these paths may have different capacity requirements. Use simple estimates to check that operation counts and data volumes make sense. Seek feedback on assumptions or system boundaries before adding detail. Early agreement prevents a lengthy discussion of a design that solves a different problem.
c03.sections.2.title: A deep dive guided by risk
c03.sections.2.body: Choose the component posing the greatest risk to the main requirements. A URL shortener needs a code uniqueness strategy; chat needs low-latency delivery and connection status; a feed needs a fan-out choice. Explain the algorithm, data model, failure conditions, and rejected alternatives. Details should have reasons: an index helps a particular access pattern, and a queue absorbs a particular spike. Avoid examining all components at equal depth. When assumptions change, adapt the design and show the consequences; revising a decision is more useful than defending the original choice without evidence.
c03.sections.3.title: Wrap-up, bottlenecks, and next steps
c03.sections.3.body: Leave time to connect the design back to the original requirements. Summarize the main decisions, name remaining bottlenecks, and explain when capacity must expand. Discuss what happens when a server dies, the network disconnects, or users grow tenfold. A good wrap-up distinguishes the current design’s capabilities from improvements still needed, such as regional replication or separating services. Do not claim all failures are solved merely because replicas exist. Name metrics that validate assumptions, such as tail latency, queue lag, or cache hit ratio.
c03.sections.4.title: Communication and collaboration practices
c03.sections.4.body: Explain the reasons for decisions in short sentences while drawing or calculating. Ask for clarification when requirements change and treat the interviewer as a design partner. Present reasonable options with their benefits and costs, then choose according to the agreed constraints. Remaining silent too long makes reasoning hard to assess, but unstructured speech also obscures decisions. Avoid jumping directly to popular solutions or adding microservices without a need. Discussion quality comes from clear connections between product requirements, architecture, and operational consequences that can be examined.
c03.sections.5.title: Managing discussion time
c03.sections.5.body: The source suggests time ranges rather than a schedule that uses all maximum values together. In a 45-minute discussion, a reasonable example is seven minutes for clarification, twelve for the initial design, twenty-two for the deep dive, and four for the wrap-up. Adjust for complexity: ambiguous requirements need more clarification, while a narrow topic allows an earlier deep dive. Use time markers to switch stages before time runs out. c06.title: Key-value store
c06.summary: Build distributed storage with partitions, replicas, quorums, versions, and failure recovery.
c06.objectives.0: Explain get and put paths from the coordinator to SSTables.
c06.objectives.1: Distinguish quorum overlap from linearizability guarantees.
c06.objectives.2: Choose conflict handling and replica repair mechanisms.
c06.sections.0.title: From one server to a distributed service
c06.sections.0.body: The basic API only needs put(key, value) and get(key), but success must be defined: is a write crash-durable, and may a read return an old version? An in-memory hash table suits one server, with compression and disks for cold data. Memory limits, CPU capacity, and the risk of losing a server drive distribution. The source design targets small pairs, low latency, automatic growth, and high availability. Removing joins from the API simplifies access but does not remove the need for versioning, durability, or failure observability.
c06.sections.1.title: CAP and consistency limits
c06.sections.1.body: During a network partition, a system cannot guarantee both a response to every request and reads that are always linearizably consistent. This is a choice during a partition rather than a rule for permanently buying two of three features. A CP system can reject requests on the side lacking authority; not every node must always stop writes. An AP system can accept operations on both sides and reconcile later. Strong, weak, and eventual consistency describe different client observations. Eventual convergence requires propagation and correct conflict resolution after the disruption ends.
c06.sections.2.title: Partitioning and replica placement
c06.sections.2.body: Consistent hashing places keys and nodes on a ring so membership changes move only some data. Virtual nodes improve distribution and allocate a larger share to higher-capacity servers. For N replicas, walk from the key position to distinct physical nodes; selecting virtual nodes on the same server adds no failure tolerance. Place replicas across failure domains and data centers as needed. A coordinator directs requests to key owners without becoming a permanent center. Rebalancing still needs bandwidth, throttling, and monitoring so adding nodes does not worsen latency.
c06.sections.3.title: Read and write quorums
c06.sections.3.body: N is the number of replicas, W the required write acknowledgements, and R the required read responses. If R + W > N on the same replica set, every read quorum intersects every write quorum. A small R speeds up reads while a large W increases write work and reduces write failure tolerance. Overlap helps read completed writes, but alone does not guarantee linearizability for concurrent writes, ambiguous versions, or sloppy quorums. Additional ordering protocols and transactions are needed for stronger guarantees. The simulator tests quorum reachability rather than proving full consistency.
c06.sections.4.title: Versions, vector clocks, and conflicts
c06.sections.4.body: Each modification can be treated as an immutable version with causal metadata. A vector clock stores a counter per writer; writers increment their counters when changing a value. X precedes Y if every counter in X is no greater than its counterpart in Y and at least one is smaller. If neither version dominates the other, they are concurrent and need application resolution. Merging shopping-cart items differs from choosing the latest profile name. Vector clocks detect causal relationships rather than automatically deciding business outcomes. Their size can grow, and pruning metadata must consider lost conflict information.
c06.sections.5.title: Failure detection and recovery
c06.sections.5.body: Gossip spreads membership and heartbeats through periodic communication among members. A late heartbeat is a suspicion rather than absolute proof that a node is dead; timeouts balance fast detection against false positives. Sloppy quorums use healthy replacement nodes to maintain operations when original replicas are unavailable. Hinted handoff stores updates for delivery when the owner recovers. Because replacement nodes may not belong to the normal replica set, R + W overlap is no longer enough. Hints need persistence, lifetimes, and measurable recovery so updates do not disappear silently.
c06.sections.6.title: Merkle trees and data center outages
c06.sections.6.body: Permanent failures or expired hints require anti-entropy. Divide the key range into buckets, hash each bucket’s contents, and combine the hashes into a Merkle tree. If roots match, the compared range does not need transfer; if they differ, traverse branches to locate different buckets and synchronize their data. Hashes only detect differences; version rules still determine repaired values. Cross-data-center replication reduces the impact of losing a location but requires quorums suited to the topology. Keep separate backups for deletions or corruption replicated to every copy.
c06.sections.7.title: Write paths, read paths, and final architecture
c06.sections.7.body: In a Cassandra-style write path, the coordinator sends mutations to replicas, replicas record the commit log and update the memtable, and the memtable eventually flushes to an SSTable. The commit log assists crash recovery; acknowledgement follows the durability policy. For reads, check memtables and caches, use Bloom filters to rule out SSTables definitely lacking the key, and merge relevant versions. Bloom filters can produce false positives and do not give the exact data location. Compaction merges SSTables and manages tombstones. Decentralized architecture removes a single mandatory coordinator but still requires repair and cluster operations.
c06.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Overlap increases and stale reads become easier to avoid.
c06.tradeoffs.0.cost: Waiting for more replicas reduces availability and adds latency.
c06.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose according to the read contract and tolerated failure count.
c06.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Replacement nodes keep accepting operations when original replicas fail.
c06.tradeoffs.1.cost: Normal overlap is lost and reconciliation becomes more complex.
c06.tradeoffs.1.when: Choose when availability matters more than strong ordering guarantees.
c06.pitfalls.0: Claiming R + W > N always means linearizability.
c06.pitfalls.1: Putting three replicas on virtual nodes belonging to one machine.
c06.pitfalls.2: Assuming a Bloom filter proves a key definitely exists.

c07.title: Unique ID generator
c07.summary: Compare ID generators and allocate Snowflake bits for capacity, time, and distributed uniqueness.
c07.objectives.0: Choose a generator based on size, ordering, and coordination.
c07.objectives.1: Calculate node capacity, sequence capacity, and timestamp lifetime.
c07.objectives.2: Handle clock rollback and duplicate worker identities.
c07.sections.0.title: A correct ID contract
c07.sections.0.body: Uniqueness, numeric format, 64-bit size, and time ordering are separate requirements. IDs that increase with time need not form a gap-free sequence; retries or failures can leave numbers unused. The source target exceeds 10,000 IDs per second, so distribution across workers and per-millisecond bursts matter. Decide whether ordering is merely an approximate global order or must be strict for every event. An ID containing time does not prove causal ordering between servers. Generator decisions follow this contract and the coordination limits allowed by the application.
c07.sections.1.title: Multi-master, UUIDs, and ticket servers
c07.sections.1.body: Multi-master can assign each database an offset and a step equal to the number of masters, but changing the master count and time ordering become complicated. UUIDs allow independent generation, but UUID families have different properties; classic random UUIDs do not meet a 64-bit numeric or time-ordering requirement. Do not conclude that every UUID version lacks time ordering. A ticket server provides a simple centralized numeric counter, but availability and throughput depend on that service. Replicating a ticket server needs coordination so failover does not issue duplicate numbers; moving the center does not automatically remove the problem.
c07.sections.2.title: The Snowflake bit layout
c07.sections.2.body: The Snowflake approach divides 64 bits into one sign bit, 41 timestamp bits in milliseconds since a custom epoch, five data center bits, five machine bits, and twelve sequence bits. The timestamp occupies the high bits so IDs tend to be time-ordered. The two location fields provide up to 1,024 worker identities, while the sequence provides 4,096 values per worker per millisecond. Uniqueness requires a combination of worker identity, timestamp, and sequence that is never reused. The system must safely allocate worker identities, including during restarts and failover.
c07.sections.3.title: Sequences, bursts, and numeric representation
c07.sections.3.body: The sequence increments for every ID with the same millisecond timestamp and returns to zero when time advances. If the sequence is exhausted, the generator must wait for the next millisecond or apply an overflow policy preserving uniqueness. The theoretical capacity of 4,096,000 IDs per second per worker is not an implementation benchmark; scheduling, clocks, and I/O may become limits earlier. In JavaScript, Number cannot exactly represent every 64-bit integer. Use BigInt inside the implementation or strings across JSON and browsers; do not round IDs into numbers that appear identical.
c07.sections.4.title: Clock synchronization and rollback
c07.sections.4.body: Timestamps based on local clocks need a policy for clock rollback. Time synchronization reduces drift, but clock adjustments or restarts can still make time lower than the last timestamp. Safe choices include stopping issuance until the clock catches up or using a logical clock with a documented drift bound. Allowing the sequence to reset to zero at an old time risks duplication. Persist or protect state according to the restart contract. Ordering across workers can also differ from the actual event order; if strict business ordering is required, use a separate ordering protocol.
c07.sections.5.title: Bit tuning and high availability
c07.sections.5.body: The total bit count is a fixed budget. Adding sequence bits increases burst capacity but reduces timestamp lifetime or worker count; adding worker bits expands distribution but leaves less room for other dimensions. A 41-bit millisecond timestamp provides about 69.7 years from the epoch, so migration must be planned before exhaustion. Generators can be distributed without a single ticket server, but the identity control plane still needs to be safe. Failover must not run two workers with the same identity simultaneously. Monitoring rollback, sequence saturation, and worker leases helps preserve uniqueness.
c07.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Snowflake avoids coordination per ID and can be distributed.
c07.tradeoffs.0.cost: It requires worker identities and clock handling.
c07.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose for high-throughput 64-bit IDs that follow time.
c07.tradeoffs.1.benefit: A larger sequence absorbs per-worker bursts.
c07.tradeoffs.1.cost: It reduces epoch lifetime if worker bits remain fixed.
c07.tradeoffs.1.when: Decide using per-millisecond bursts rather than daily averages.
c07.pitfalls.0: Assuming time-ordered IDs always indicate causal order.
c07.pitfalls.1: Activating two workers with the same identity during failover.

c07.exercise.prompt: A worker receives a burst of 5,000 IDs in one millisecond with a 12-bit sequence. What happens, and how can the design improve?
c07.exercise.solution: There are 4,096 slots in one millisecond, so 904 IDs cannot yet be issued with the same timestamp. The generator waits for the next time window or distributes load across workers with unique identities. Increasing the sequence to 13 bits provides 8,192 slots, but one bit must come from timestamps or workers in a fixed 64-bit layout. Choose based on bursts and worker count; monitor queues and rollback so capacity optimization does not sacrifice uniqueness.

c08.title: URL shortener
c08.summary: Design unique short codes, fast redirect paths, and analytics without conflating encoding with hashing.
c08.objectives.0: Compare base62 with hashing and collision resolution.
c08.objectives.1: Choose redirects based on caching and analytics requirements.
c08.objectives.2: Calculate code length and database load after caching.
c08.sections.0.title: Requirements, capacity, and APIs
c08.sections.0.body: The service accepts a long URL through POST and returns a short URL, then translates the short code through GET into a redirect. The source uses 100 million new URLs per day, ten-year retention, and a 10:1 read-to-write ratio. That produces 365 billion mappings; assuming one KB per mapping gives about 365 TB logically. Define policies for custom aliases, expiration, deletion, and whether the same URL always receives the same code. Validate URL schemes and input length so the service does not create redirects to disallowed protocols.
c08.sections.1.title: 301 and 302 redirects
c08.sections.1.body: A 301 redirect indicates a permanent move and can be heuristically cached, so some subsequent clicks may go directly to the destination. A 302 redirect indicates a temporary move and is usually chosen when the service needs to observe clicks and change destinations. Cache-Control policies still matter; the status code alone does not guarantee that all requests reach the server or are always cached. The service cannot perfectly reconstruct analytics bypassed by caching. Decide whether destinations can change and how complete measurement must be before choosing a suitable status and redirect TTL.
c08.sections.2.title: Data model and mapping creation
c08.sections.2.body: Store the id, short code, and long URL, with a unique constraint on the short code and indexes for lookup patterns. Checking an existing URL before creating a code helps deduplication, but two concurrent requests can both pass the check; transactions or constraints handle the race. With an ID strategy, request a unique ID, encode it as base62, and durably store the mapping before returning the result. Reverse lookups for long URLs can use a digest plus verification against the original URL. Deduplication policies must consider accounts, expiry, and analytics because the same destination does not necessarily mean the same product link.
c08.sections.3.title: Base62 versus hashing with collisions
c08.sections.3.body: Base62 converts integers into characters 0–9, a–z, and A–Z. With unique IDs and one-to-one encoding, codes do not collide, but length grows with the ID and sequential patterns may be easy to guess. Truncated URL hashes have fixed length but can still collide. Resolve this using new candidates and atomic inserts rather than relying on low probability. Bloom filters help reject some lookups that are definitely absent, but positive results must be verified in storage. A hash is not reversible; the mapping database provides the destination URL.
c08.sections.4.title: Read paths, caching, and scaling
c08.sections.4.body: On a click, the load balancer sends the request to the stateless web tier. Look up the short code in cache; on a miss, read the database, populate the cache, and send the redirect. Negative caching can absorb random-code attacks, but its TTL should be short so new codes are not considered missing for too long. Hot links may need distributed caching and stampede control. The database uses replication for reads and sharding for mapping capacity; code-based routing must be deterministic. Link changes or deletion need invalidation consistent with the TTL and product contract.
c08.sections.5.title: Abuse, analytics, and reliability
c08.sections.5.body: Rate limiting restricts link creation and probing by IP or identity, with a separate policy for public clicks. Detecting harmful destinations and controlling administrative access are part of service operations. Send analytics asynchronously so logging does not add redirect latency, with stated tolerance for loss or duplication. Replication, backups, and recovery protect mappings, while the ID service must remain unique during failover. Monitor hit ratio, database latency, and redirect failure rate. Code-space capacity is not the only limit; networks and hot keys may become bottlenecks first.
c08.tradeoffs.0.cost: An ID generator is needed and codes may be easy to guess.
c08.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose when deterministic uniqueness matters more than fixed length.
c08.tradeoffs.1.cost: Clicks bypassing the service reduce analytics visibility and destination flexibility.
c08.tradeoffs.1.when: Choose 301 for permanent destinations; configure 302 and cache policies for dynamic links.
c08.pitfalls.0: Assuming a short hash can be reversed without a database.
c08.pitfalls.1: Assuming Bloom filters guarantee codes never collide.
c08.pitfalls.2: Assuming 302 alone guarantees every click is recorded.

Use a safe ID generator, a unique constraint on the code, caching for redirects, and an analytics queue. Plan for peak traffic and hot links separately from average figures.

c09.title: Web crawler
c09.summary: Combine frontiers, priority, politeness, deduplication, and freshness to collect the web in a controlled way.
c09.objectives.0: Explain the crawl pipeline from seeds to storage.
c09.objectives.1: Calculate host, worker, and politeness-delay bottlenecks.
c09.objectives.2: Control duplicate content, spider traps, and recrawling.
c09.sections.0.title: Crawling goals and boundaries
c09.sections.0.body: Crawlers are used for search indexes, archiving, data mining, and change monitoring. Each requires different coverage and freshness. The source focuses on HTML, one billion pages per month, ignoring duplicates, and five-year retention. Its four main qualities are scalability, robustness, politeness, and extensibility. A storage estimate of about 30 PB depends on assumed page size and crawl rate; state the size explicitly before using that figure. Define access rules, excluded content, recrawling, and treatment of dynamic pages so the scope remains operationally manageable.
c09.sections.1.title: The pipeline from seeds to the frontier
c09.sections.1.body: Seed URLs start exploration and are chosen to represent relevant topics or locations. The frontier stores scheduled URLs; the downloader resolves DNS and fetches HTML. The parser validates content, content-hash checks detect duplicates, and content storage saves new pages. The extractor discovers links, the filter removes disallowed or irrelevant URLs, and the URL-seen check avoids repeat visits. URL storage records visit status. Every stage needs task identities and checkpoints so crashes neither lose progress nor cause URLs to be processed endlessly.
c09.sections.2.title: The web graph, priority, and freshness
c09.sections.2.body: The web is a directed graph with pages as nodes and hyperlinks as edges. BFS explores more broadly than DFS, which can become trapped in very deep branches, but ordinary BFS does not consider page value. Front queues can divide candidates by priority estimated from quality, popularity, or update frequency. The scheduler gives important queues more opportunities while preserving fairness. Freshness requires recrawling based on change history and importance rather than assuming URL-seen means a page never needs another visit. Store crawl times and the next visit schedule.
c09.sections.3.title: Back queues and per-host politeness
c09.sections.3.body: The frontier needs two dimensions: front queues for priority and back queues for host limits. The router places URLs from one host into the same queue; the selector chooses only hosts eligible for access again. One active request per host and delays between downloads are safe training policies, although deployments can set other limits. Adding workers does not increase throughput if all URLs come from a few hosts. Store next-eligible-time and avoid repeated immediate retries. Fairness prevents domains with millions of links from monopolizing the crawler and reducing coverage of smaller domains.
c09.sections.4.title: Downloaders, robots, and efficiency
c09.sections.4.body: The downloader checks robots.txt rules, uses a DNS cache, sets timeouts, and handles redirects with clear limits. The Robots Exclusion Protocol supplies crawler access rules rather than authorization to read protected content. Robots caches have lifetimes, and fetch failures must be handled according to protocol policy. Geographic distribution can reduce network travel, but host assignments must preserve global politeness limits. Short timeouts free workers from stalled hosts at the risk of missing slow pages. Limit response sizes, content types, and redirect counts so one page cannot exhaust resources.
c09.sections.5.title: Robustness, extensibility, and problematic content
c09.sections.5.body: Consistent hashing can distribute host ownership among servers with controlled movement when membership changes. Catch parser and downloader errors per task so one malformed HTML page does not crash the process. Separate parsing, filtering, and storage modules so image support or monitoring can be added. Content hashes reduce exact duplication; different URLs can still have the same content. Spider traps such as endless calendars require depth limits, URL-length limits, and per-domain budgets. Filter spam and tracking parameters carefully because excessive normalization can merge pages that are actually different.
c09.sections.6.title: Storage, scaling, and observability
c09.sections.6.body: Store HTML in object storage and crawl metadata in shardable storage, with indexes for status, time, and host. Replication supports availability, while checkpoints and durable queues allow stateless workers to recover. JavaScript rendering needs a separate path because CPU and network costs are far greater than fetching HTML; the source raises it as a further consideration. Crawl analytics measure success, duplicate ratio, timeouts, freshness, and per-host queues. Scale according to the actual bottleneck: workers, bandwidth, active host count, parsers, or storage, while preserving politeness as capacity grows.
c09.tradeoffs.0.cost: Other domains or topics may be delayed.
c09.tradeoffs.0.when: Use weighted scheduling with starvation limits.
c09.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Workers help when many hosts can be accessed in parallel.
c09.tradeoffs.1.cost: They are ineffective when host limits are the bottleneck.
c09.tradeoffs.1.when: Expand workers only after checking politeness throughput.
c09.pitfalls.0: Assuming every seen URL can be banned forever, eliminating recrawling.
c09.pitfalls.1: Assuming more workers permit more requests to one host.
c09.pitfalls.2: Conflating URL deduplication with content deduplication.

Adding workers does not help. You need more eligible hosts, a delay reduction consistent with host policies, or a lower throughput target. The frontier still maintains separate per-host queues; the scheduler must not violate politeness to meet the global target.

c10.title: Notification system
c10.summary: Send push, SMS, and email through durable queues with user preferences, retries, and deduplication.
c10.objectives.0: Separate event acceptance from delivery on each channel.
c10.objectives.1: Calculate retry amplification and backlog growth.
c10.objectives.2: Explain durability, idempotency, consent, and delivery status.
c10.sections.0.title: Scope and notification types
c10.sections.0.body: Push, SMS, and email notifications have different destination addresses, provider limits, and delivery characteristics. The source targets soft real-time: small delays are desirable, but hard deadlines are not promised. Example daily volumes are ten million push notifications, one million SMS messages, and five million emails. Define transactional versus promotional notifications, priorities, schedules, expiry, and user opt-out preferences. API acceptance is not the same as displaying a message on a device. The product contract must distinguish accepted, queued, provider accepted, delivered, and opened so success is not inferred too early.
c10.sections.1.title: User contacts and provider adapters
c10.sections.1.body: During signup or installation, collect emails, phone numbers, and device tokens with appropriate validation and consent rules. One user may have many tokens, and tokens can change or become invalid; store platform, update time, and active status. APNs and FCM are the push paths illustrated by the source, while SMS and email use separate provider adapters. Adapters translate internal payloads into provider formats and classify transient and permanent errors. Do not put provider details in every trigger service because switching providers would spread changes across the entire application.
c10.sections.2.title: From one server to a queue architecture
c10.sections.2.body: The initial design has trigger services, a notification server that validates and fetches metadata, and an external provider. One server becomes a failure point and combines rendering, storage, and delivery costs. Improve it with a stateless notification API, separate databases and caches, and durable queues per channel or priority. Workers take tasks and contact providers, so spikes do not block callers. Scale APIs and workers independently. Queues absorb spikes but do not eliminate sustained overload; queue lag grows when the arrival rate exceeds effective delivery capacity.
c10.sections.3.title: Durability, retries, and deduplication
c10.sections.3.body: Persist events and status before acknowledging acceptance; transactional outboxes help combine business changes with task publication. Workers acknowledge tasks only after results are stored according to the contract. Retries use backoff, jitter, attempt limits, and dead-letter queues for errors that remain unsuccessful. Event IDs support deduplication, but a simple check-then-send still has races and crash windows. Use atomic claims and provider idempotency keys where available. If a provider accepts a message but its response is lost, retrying may resend it. Exactly-once display to users is not an automatic queue guarantee.
c10.sections.4.title: Templates, preferences, and rate limiting
c10.sections.4.body: Templates separate content from events and support languages, versions, and validated parameters. During rendering, avoid missing parameters and limit included personal data. Notification settings store allowed channels; check preferences at enqueue time and, for delayed messages, again before delivery. Per-user rate limiters curb spam, while provider limiters respect external throughput. Priorities keep OTPs or important alerts from being delayed by promotional campaigns. Old messages can lose value, so expiry and coalescing multiple updates are necessary. Template and contact caches need invalidation when users change their data.
c10.sections.5.title: Monitoring, event tracking, and security
c10.sections.5.body: Monitor queue length, oldest-message age, retry rate, provider latency, invalid tokens, and dead-letter counts. Queue lag guides scaling decisions better than worker CPU alone. Event tracking connects acceptance, delivery callbacks, opens, and clicks through event IDs, but engagement metrics are not always available or accurate on every channel. Protect APIs with service authentication and authorization for notification types; store provider credentials in secret storage rather than clients or logs. Validate provider callbacks and access to user preferences. Log retention should support troubleshooting without unnecessarily storing sensitive content.
c10.sections.6.title: The final flow and capacity optimization
c10.sections.6.body: A trigger sends an event, the API validates and retrieves metadata, the durable event enters a queue, workers check preferences and expiry, and an adapter sends to the provider and records the result. Callbacks update status idempotently. Horizontal scaling and caching help, but final capacity remains limited by provider quotas and external failures. Geographic distribution can reduce latency and failure domains if cross-region routing and deduplication are designed correctly. The term distributed crawling in the source’s wrap-up is not relevant to notification pipelines; distributing delivery workers is the relevant optimization. Test queue recovery and provider outages rather than only normal throughput.

c10.tradeoffs.0.cost: Extra attempts consume quotas and can duplicate messages.
c10.tradeoffs.0.when: Use limits and backoff based on errors and message expiry.
c10.tradeoffs.1.choice: One queue versus queues per channel/priority
c10.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Separation isolates slow providers and protects important messages.
c10.tradeoffs.1.cost: It requires more configuration and fairness policies.
c10.tradeoffs.1.when: Choose when latency requirements or provider limits differ.
c10.pitfalls.0: Assuming provider acceptance means the user has read the message.
c10.pitfalls.1: Marking an event seen before sending without a recovery state machine.
c10.pitfalls.2: Adding workers beyond provider quotas and causing more retries.

c10.exercise.solution: Three total attempts yield an average of 1 + 0.2 + 0.04 = 1.24 attempts per message. Demand becomes 124 attempts/s, exceeding the 120/s quota. c11.title: News Feed System
c11.summary: Build a chronological feed with hybrid fanout, queues, and caches that separate identifiers from post content.
c11.objectives.0: Separate feed publishing and reading flows.
c11.objectives.1: Calculate the costs of push, pull, and hybrid fanout.
c11.objectives.2: Design caches and recovery for delayed fanout.
c11.sections.0.title: Scope, ordering, and APIs
c11.sections.0.body: Start with two capabilities: users create posts and read posts from their connections. The source assumes web and mobile clients, ten million daily active users, at most five thousand friends, and reverse chronological ordering. These are design assumptions, not facts about a particular service’s size. POST /v1/me/feed accepts content; GET retrieves the feed belonging to the authenticated identity. Use a timestamp cursor together with an ID to keep pagination stable as new posts arrive. Photos and videos are stored as media references, so feed responses do not carry entire large files.
c11.sections.1.title: Publishing path
c11.sections.1.body: A load balancer routes requests to stateless web servers. The server checks authentication, authorization, and spam limits before the post service stores a post. After storage succeeds, fanout work enters a queue and notification services can run separately. Separating writes from distribution keeps publishing responses fast even when there are many friends. Record events reliably alongside post changes, then make workers idempotent using the user-and-post pair. Otherwise, a failure between storage and enqueueing can produce a post that never appears in feeds.
c11.sections.2.title: Push, pull, and a hybrid approach
c11.sections.2.body: Fanout on write places post IDs in friends’ feeds immediately after publication; readers receive a ready-made list. However, one popular account can generate millions of jobs, and many recipients never read them. Fanout on read gathers connections’ posts when the feed is requested, reducing wasted work but increasing read cost. A hybrid design uses push for ordinary accounts and pull for highly connected accounts. Choose the threshold from posting rate, the proportion of active readers, and worker capacity, rather than simply labeling an account a celebrity.
c11.sections.3.title: Workers and feed limits
c11.sections.3.body: The fanout service reads relationships from the social graph and then checks settings such as muting and restricted sharing. The queue contains a post ID and eligible recipients; workers add post-and-user pairs to the cache. Store only a limited number of recent posts to control memory use. Lists of full objects would duplicate content and complicate changes. When users open older pages, the system needs a fallback to durable storage or must rebuild the list. Relationship changes and post deletion still need to be checked when constructing the response.
c11.sections.4.title: Reading and five cache layers
c11.sections.4.body: The feed service retrieves IDs from the news feed cache, merges posts from accounts using pull, and then sorts and hydrates details in batches. The content cache holds post content; a hot cache can protect viral posts. The social graph cache holds connections, the action cache holds interactions, and the counter cache holds counts of likes, replies, and followers. The five layers have different update patterns and staleness tolerances. Avoid one database request per post. Caching IDs speeds up list retrieval, but access permissions and content existence must still be verified before display.
c11.sections.5.title: Scale, reliability, and observability
c11.sections.5.body: The stateless web tier is easy to expand; the database can use shards and read replicas. Distributing caches with consistent hashing limits data movement when nodes change. Queues absorb spikes but do not remove the cost of work, so monitor the oldest message’s age, backlog, and time until a post becomes visible. Cache hit rate and percentile latency help distinguish reading problems from distribution problems. Retries with deduplication prevent duplicate IDs. If a cache is lost, gradual reconstruction prevents all users from flooding the database at once; a slightly delayed feed is more reasonable than a total failure.
c11.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Push makes reads short; pull avoids distribution to inactive users.
c11.tradeoffs.0.cost: Push increases write amplification; pull adds merging at read time.
c11.tradeoffs.0.when: Use a hybrid approach when connection counts are highly skewed.
c11.tradeoffs.1.benefit: IDs save memory and centralize content versions.
c11.tradeoffs.1.cost: Details must be retrieved and merged.
c11.tradeoffs.1.when: Choose IDs when posts can change and appear in many feeds.
c11.pitfalls.0: Assuming successful enqueueing means all friends see the post immediately.
c11.pitfalls.1: Storing a full object copy for every recipient.
c11.pitfalls.2: Ignoring muting, deletion, and permission changes on the read path.

c12.title: Chat System
c12.summary: Separate WebSocket connections, message history, device synchronization, and presence so chat can recover from disconnections.
c12.objectives.0: Choose a communication protocol and manage stateful servers.
c12.objectives.1: Explain message ordering and multi-device synchronization.
c12.objectives.2: Measure group fanout and presence heartbeat costs.
c12.sections.0.title: Requirements and communication protocols
c12.sections.0.body: The source’s scope includes one-to-one chat, groups of up to one hundred members, presence, multiple devices, push notifications, and permanent history for fifty million daily active users. Simple polling generates many empty requests; long polling holds a request until a message is available but still requires reconnect management. WebSocket provides a persistent bidirectional channel for sending and receiving. This choice does not eliminate the need for HTTP for login, profiles, and history retrieval. Limit message size and use backpressure so slow connections do not fill server memory.
c12.sections.1.title: Stateless and stateful services
c12.sections.1.body: Signup, login, and profile APIs can be stateless, while chat servers hold user connections and routing state. Service discovery selects a server based on location and capacity; the source uses ZooKeeper as an example of coordination. Presence and push notifications become separate services with different workloads. A load balancer distributes new connections; it does not magically move existing ones. When shutting down a server, mark it as draining, stop accepting new connections, and ask clients to reconnect. Store history outside the chat process so losing a server does not lose acknowledged messages.
c12.sections.2.title: Data model and message ordering
c12.sections.2.body: History can be partitioned in a key-value store by conversation. Group messages use a channel_id and message_id pair so history reads become ordered ranges. Global IDs such as Snowflake provide uniqueness, while a local sequence is sufficient when ordering is only needed within one channel. ID uniqueness alone does not establish causal ordering across all senders. Decide when the server acknowledges a message: after it is durable, not merely received by a socket. Client deduplication keys support retries, and cursors must match the ordering scope so multi-channel users do not miss messages.
c12.sections.3.title: Direct delivery and group fanout
c12.sections.3.body: The sender connects to the first chat server, which assigns a message identity and stores the message. Routing knows the recipient’s server; online users receive delivery through active connections, while offline users may receive a push notification. For small groups, the message or a reference is copied into each recipient’s inbox to simplify synchronization. Cost grows with members and devices, so this approach does not automatically suit enormous public channels. Sent, received by a device, and read are distinct events. Queues and retries require deduplication to handle disconnections after an acknowledgement is lost.
c12.sections.4.title: Device synchronization and presence
c12.sections.4.body: Each device stores its last message position and requests messages addressed to the user with newer positions. For local sequences, keep a cursor per conversation; for a user’s ordered inbox, keep an inbox cursor. Periodic heartbeats maintain presence, and a timeout threshold marks users offline. Online status is an estimate that can lag because of mobile networking. Presence changes can be published to friend-relationship channels, which works well for small groups but is expensive for highly connected users. Do not assume every device must receive every friend’s heartbeat on every interval.
c12.sections.5.title: Scale, failures, and extensions
c12.sections.5.body: Add chat servers for connections and shard history for storage load; caches speed up session lookup and recent reads. Retries, queues, and reconnections must carry cursors so missed messages can be retrieved. Monitor connections, outbound queues, acknowledgement latency, and reconnect rates to detect overloaded servers. Media requires object storage and compression, while end-to-end encryption changes key management and message search. Client caching and geographic distribution improve the experience, but they do not replace reliable history storage.
c12.tradeoffs.0.benefit: WebSocket avoids many empty requests and supports bidirectional communication.
c12.tradeoffs.0.cost: Servers maintain connections, backpressure, and reconnect handling.
c12.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose it for real-time chat with long-lived active connections.
c12.tradeoffs.1.choice: Per-recipient inbox versus shared group log
c12.tradeoffs.1.cost: Write amplification increases with group membership.
c12.tradeoffs.1.when: Inboxes suit small groups; shared logs are more suitable for large channels.
c12.pitfalls.0: Treating push notifications as message storage.
c12.pitfalls.1: Using a single global cursor for local sequences in many channels.
c12.pitfalls.2: Treating a delayed heartbeat as definite proof that a user has left.

c12.exercise.prompt: A user sends a message while the recipient’s phone is offline but their laptop is online. Explain delivery and recovery when the laptop’s server fails.
c12.exercise.hints.1: Keep cursors outside the socket connection.
c12.exercise.solution: The message is durably stored and recorded in the recipient’s inbox before acknowledging it to the sender. Routing delivers it to the online laptop; push policy can avoid excessive phone notifications when the user is active. If the laptop’s server fails before delivery acknowledgement, the client reconnects to another server through discovery and sends its last cursor. The server retrieves newer messages from the inbox. Retries may cause redelivery, so the client deduplicates by message_id. Laptop presence ends after the timeout; history does not depend on that session.
