c13.title: Search Autocomplete
c13.summary: Serve top-k suggestions from an asynchronously built trie while managing freshness, filtering, and prefix distribution.
c13.objectives.0: Explain prefix search and trie top-k caching.
c13.objectives.1: Design a pipeline from logs to trie snapshots.
c13.objectives.2: Compare ranking freshness with update costs.
c13.sections.0.title: Scope and latency budget
c13.sections.0.body: Autocomplete provides suggestions as users type, rather than executing a full search. The source limits results to five, ranks by popularity, supports lowercase English letters, and targets responses below one hundred milliseconds. Ten million active users can generate many requests per search because each prefix triggers a call. Separate the latency-sensitive query service from heavy data gathering. Debouncing or discarding old responses keeps results from being mixed up when users type quickly. The example’s log-growth and QPS figures are exercise assumptions that need recalculation for real input patterns.
c13.sections.1.title: Trie and top-k at each node
c13.sections.1.body: A trie stores character paths so identical prefixes share nodes. The basic approach finds the prefix node, traverses the entire subtree, collects candidates, and sorts frequencies to select top-k. This is costly for short prefixes such as a single letter. Storing the five best candidates at every node reduces the read path to locating the prefix and reading a small list. It trades memory and build work for query latency. Limit prefix length, but do not regard prefix traversal as truly constant if input length is unbounded; traversal still depends on the characters processed.
c13.sections.2.title: Log collection and snapshots
c13.sections.2.body: Updating a trie on every keystroke is difficult to sustain at high volume. Write final queries or defined events to an append-only analytics log, then let an aggregator build a frequency table. Workers build the trie and publish new versions asynchronously, for example weekly for stable data. The trie cache holds a version ready for reading; the database stores a structured snapshot or prefix/node-data pairs. Switch the version pointer after validating the build so queries never see a half-built structure. Keep the previous version for rollback and define log-retention rules and protection for sensitive query data.
c13.sections.3.title: Queries, filters, and deletion
c13.sections.3.body: The query service locates the prefix node, retrieves top-k, checks filters, and constructs a lightweight response. AJAX and browser caches reduce network round trips, but client caches need age limits and versions. Filters let inappropriate suggestions be hidden immediately without waiting for the next trie build. Physical deletion can follow asynchronously; filter policies must also apply to server and client caches. If every cached top-k result is blocked, provide additional candidates or accept fewer results. Deleting strings without rebuilding rankings can leave stale references at prefix nodes.
c13.sections.4.title: Sharding and availability
c13.sections.4.body: A trie can be partitioned by prefix range, with queries routed using a shard map manager. Splitting a–m versus n–z is easy to understand, but language frequencies are uneven; popular prefixes need further subdivision or additional replicas. Measure query load and node size, not just letter counts. Cache replicas and durable snapshots speed up recovery. If a shard fails, a client may receive an empty list or an older version with a clearly defined freshness limit. Building the entire trie simultaneously on every node risks flooding storage during restarts.
c13.sections.5.title: Languages, regions, and trends
c13.sections.5.body: Unicode expands the alphabet, but normalization, accents, tokenization, and spelling forms need consistent policies between logging and lookup. Tries per country or language produce more relevant rankings while adding versions to manage. Weekly historical popularity is stable but slow to capture new events. Shorter aggregation windows or weights favoring recent activity improve trending suggestions at greater build cost and with more manipulation risk. Separate a trends overlay from the main snapshot when rapid updates are needed. Evaluate suggestion quality and abuse as well as latency; the most frequent ranking is not always the most helpful.
c13.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Cached top-k avoids scanning candidates on every query.
c13.tradeoffs.0.cost: Memory use and ranking updates increase.
c13.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose caching for hot prefixes with strict latency targets.
c13.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Snapshots are stable; overlays respond to rapid changes.
c13.tradeoffs.1.cost: An overlay adds merging, moderation, and version state.
c13.tradeoffs.1.when: Use an overlay when suggestions depend on current events.
c13.pitfalls.0: Treating every keystroke as an equivalent final query in statistics.
c13.pitfalls.1: Assuming letter ranges guarantee balanced shards.
c13.pitfalls.2: Waiting for a weekly build to remove prohibited suggestions.

c13.exercise.hints.0: Move sorting to the build, rather than the request.

Log final queries, aggregate hourly for a trends overlay, and merge overlay candidates with the snapshot’s top-k at query time. Apply filtering after merging and before responding. Build full snapshots off the query path, validate quality, and then switch versions atomically. Monitor build duration so the one-hour window does not create backlog, and retain the previous snapshot for rollback.

c14.title: Youtube
c14.summary: Separate uploads, DAG transcoding, and CDN streaming to control queues, quality, and bandwidth costs.
c14.objectives.0: Explain separate upload and streaming flows.
c14.objectives.1: Design a DAG transcoding scheduler that supports retries.
c14.objectives.2: Calculate worker needs and origin bandwidth.
c14.sections.0.title: Scope and media estimates
c14.sections.0.body: The design focuses on fast uploads, smooth playback, quality choices, controlled costs, and availability on mobile devices, browsers, and televisions. Historical statistics in the source provide context, while the exercise assumes five million daily users and an average video size of three hundred MB. Calculate storage from the number of uploads, not views. Calculate egress from actual playback duration and bitrate because not every view downloads an entire video. Metadata APIs have different requirements from large-file transfers; separating them prevents video from consuming user-interaction service capacity.
c14.sections.1.title: Original uploads and metadata
c14.sections.1.body: The client uploads a video to original blob storage and sends metadata to the API in parallel. Metadata records processing status, so a file is not considered ready merely because its title has been stored. A queue triggers transcoding; after outputs are stored, a completion event changes the status and notifies the user. Completion handlers must be idempotent when events are redelivered. Chunk-based uploads support resumption after network failures, and upload centers near users reduce transfer time. Signed URLs restrict the upload’s object, action, and expiration, while the API remains responsible for authorization and size limits.
c14.sections.2.title: Streaming and formats
c14.sections.2.body: Ready-to-play videos are distributed through a CDN; players fetch segments directly from the edge while APIs handle metadata and permissions. HLS and MPEG-DASH provide manifests and bitrate variants so clients can adjust quality to network conditions. Containers such as MP4 wrap audio, video, and metadata, while codecs such as H.264 or VP9 define compression. They are not interchangeable terms. Provide combinations supported by target devices, choose segment durations, and measure startup and rebuffering. A high CDN hit rate reduces origin load, but egress to viewers still exists.
c14.sections.3.title: Video-processing DAG
c14.sections.3.body: Transcoding is expensive because one video produces many resolutions, bitrates, and codecs. A DAG describes dependencies: splitting audio/video/metadata precedes encoding, while thumbnails and watermarks can run in parallel when their inputs are available. The preprocessor splits videos at GOP boundaries so workers can operate on decodable chunks. Store temporary chunks and metadata for retries without reuploading. The DAG comes from configuration, and the scheduler divides it into stages. Do not add every task’s duration to calculate final latency when tasks run in parallel; latency follows the longest dependency path and resource queues.
c14.sections.4.title: Resource manager and resilience
c14.sections.4.body: The resource manager has a task queue, information about available workers, and a running queue binding tasks to workers. The scheduler chooses pairings based on resource needs and utilization; audio, video, and thumbnail workers may differ. Task persistence and leases help detect dead workers and retry work. Outputs are written to temporary locations before final publication so retries do not corrupt results. Temporary errors such as storage disruptions can be retried with backoff, while corrupt files are stopped with a clear message. Queues between modules increase parallelism but require backlog observability and temporary-data cleanup.
c14.sections.5.title: Speed, security, and cost optimizations
c14.sections.5.body: Parallel uploads and processing shorten readiness time as long as bandwidth and workers do not become new bottlenecks. Encryption, DRM, and watermarking protect different aspects: transfer confidentiality, playback restrictions, and copy identification. Less popular videos can be served from a high-capacity origin or encoded on demand to save storage, at the cost of slower startup. Regional distribution based on popularity avoids rarely used caches. Custom CDNs or ISP partnerships can reduce costs at large scale but add network operations. Measure costs together with playback quality rather than separately.
c14.tradeoffs.0.choice: Encode all variants versus on demand
c14.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Pre-encoding makes videos immediately available at many quality levels.
c14.tradeoffs.0.cost: Compute and storage are used for variants that may never be watched.
c14.tradeoffs.0.when: Pre-encode popular videos; use on-demand encoding for the long tail when delay is acceptable.
c14.tradeoffs.1.choice: Broad CDN coverage versus origin for cold videos
c14.tradeoffs.1.benefit: A CDN brings video closer to viewers and reduces origin traffic.
c14.tradeoffs.1.cost: Distribution and caching are less efficient for rarely accessed content.
c14.tradeoffs.1.when: Prioritize caching according to regional popularity.
c14.pitfalls.0: Confusing a container with a codec.
c14.pitfalls.1: Assuming a CDN hit removes egress costs to viewers.
c14.pitfalls.2: Marking a video ready before all important outputs are stored.

Add spare capacity for retries and spikes; this result ignores codec differences and overhead. Original uploads and pending metadata run in parallel. The preprocessor splits GOPs and builds the DAG, the scheduler assigns tasks to workers, outputs are stored, and then the completion handler updates status while the CDN retrieves segments. If a worker fails, retry from temporary data. Measure backlog in media minutes so autoscaling follows actual work rather than just video counts.

c15.title: Google Drive
c15.summary: Synchronize files using blocks, version metadata, and notifications without losing changes during conflicts or offline periods.
c15.objectives.0: Separate file blocks from consistent metadata.
c15.objectives.1: Explain delta synchronization, versions, and cross-device conflicts.
c15.objectives.2: Calculate transfer savings and the consequences of block size.
c15.sections.0.title: Scope, namespaces, and APIs
c15.sections.0.body: A file-storage service needs uploads, downloads, device synchronization, revisions, permissioned sharing, and change notifications. Data loss is unacceptable, while synchronization speed and bandwidth efficiency determine the user experience. The initial design uses a web server, a namespace directory per user, and a metadata database; file identity combines a namespace and path. This is a starting point rather than a system that withstands large scale. APIs support direct uploads for small files, resumable sessions for large files, downloads, and revision lists. Offline users need a way to catch up on changes that does not depend on transient notifications.
c15.sections.1.title: From one server to distributed blocks
c15.sections.1.body: Shard storage and metadata by user identity or namespace, then keep file data in replicated object storage. Block servers divide files into blocks of at most four MB in the source’s example, assign hashes, compress and encrypt them, and store blocks independently. A manifest preserves block order for reconstruction. Stateless APIs handle authentication and metadata; a load balancer distributes traffic. Metadata caching speeds lookup without replacing the database. Replication and cold storage help reliability and cost, but placement decisions must account for recovery time and user access patterns.
c15.sections.2.title: Metadata schema and uploads
c15.sections.2.body: The user table stores identity, the file table stores namespace/path/size, the block table maps hashes and locations, and the version table stores revision manifests. When an upload starts, metadata is pending. Blocks are uploaded and verified, and completion marks a version uploaded only after required blocks are available. Notifications follow once the version can be downloaded. Callbacks must be idempotent, and abandoned pending uploads need safe cleanup. Because metadata and object storage do not share an ordinary transaction, use a state machine and reconciliation so retries or lost events do not create apparently complete files with missing blocks.
c15.sections.3.title: Delta synchronization and conflicts
c15.sections.3.body: Delta synchronization sends changed blocks, reducing transfer when edits are small relative to the file. Compression depends on file type; already compressed video does not automatically shrink much. Two devices may edit the same base version. Compare the submitted version with the server version; the first change can be accepted, while the next becomes a conflict copy for the user to merge or choose. Do not silently overwrite changes. For revisions, retain references to unchanged blocks and store a new manifest. Garbage collection discards blocks only when no version or share still references them.
c15.sections.4.title: Downloads, notifications, and offline users
c15.sections.4.body: Online devices learn about changes from the notification service, which uses long polling in the source’s design. After a signal, the client requests the latest version’s metadata, downloads blocks it does not yet have, and assembles the file according to the manifest. Offline devices catch up through a change record or backup queue when they reconnect. Notifications are hints to synchronize, not the source of truth for all revisions. Use a durable cursor so reconnections can retrieve missed changes. Sharing permissions must be checked for metadata and block access; knowing a file hash must not automatically grant download rights.
c15.sections.5.title: Storage optimization and recovery
c15.sections.5.body: Hash-based deduplication at the account level reduces copies of identical blocks; limit revisions using a retention policy visible to users. Inactive files can move to cold storage with an explanation of restoration time. When a block server fails, pending tasks are reassigned; when a database primary fails, failover must preserve metadata versions so they do not silently regress. Backup load balancers, notification reconnection, and cross-region storage replicas improve availability. Test file recovery from metadata and blocks, not just server health. Design encryption and deduplication together because different ciphertext can defeat similarity detection.
c15.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Small blocks reduce transfer for scattered edits.
c15.tradeoffs.0.cost: There are more hashes, manifests, requests, and overhead.
c15.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose based on edit patterns and request costs, not only file size.
c15.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Conflict copies preserve both parties’ changes.
c15.tradeoffs.1.cost: Users must choose or merge the results.
c15.tradeoffs.1.when: Use them for general files without a safe semantic merge algorithm.
c15.pitfalls.0: Assuming notifications always arrive and are sufficient for synchronization.
c15.pitfalls.1: Deleting blocks still referenced by other revisions.
c15.pitfalls.2: Equating a content hash with permission to access the content.

c15.exercise.solution: The first laptop uploads two new blocks and a manifest referencing the base revision. The server accepts the revision after all blocks are available. The second laptop comes online and sends the old base version; version checking detects a conflict. Save the second manifest as a conflict copy so edits are not lost, then let the user merge or choose. Identical blocks do not need retransferring if their hashes are already present in the account. Notifications inform other devices, but a change cursor is still used on reconnect. Old revisions retain block references until retention expires.

c16.title: Proximity Service
c16.summary: Find nearby businesses with spatial indexes, neighboring-cell coverage, and precise distance filtering.
c16.objectives.0: Compare grids, geohashes, quadtrees, and S2.
c16.objectives.1: Explain cell candidates versus results within the radius.
c16.objectives.2: Design caches and business-location index updates.
c16.sections.0.title: Scope, APIs, and the business model
c16.sections.0.body: A proximity service searches for businesses by latitude, longitude, and radius, provides business details, and accepts owner updates that need not appear immediately. The source’s example uses one hundred million active users and two hundred million businesses; calculate QPS from searches per user and leave headroom for busy hours. The nearby endpoint differs from business CRUD. Separate the business_id detail table from the spatial index mapping cells to IDs. Business locations are relatively stable, so read replicas and batch-built indexes can be used with a clear lag limit, unlike tracking moving friends.
c16.sections.1.title: Read architecture and naive search
c16.sections.1.body: A load balancer routes searches to a stateless location-based service and details and updates to a business service. The primary database accepts changes, and replicas handle read-heavy traffic. Bounding-box search using latitude and longitude columns provides a baseline, but two one-dimensional indexes do not automatically provide efficient radius searches. The box also includes points outside the circle. Latitude and longitude are angles, so a radius in meters cannot be added directly without conversion. Spatial indexes narrow down candidates; calculate actual distances afterward to ensure correct results.
c16.sections.2.title: Fixed grids and geohashes
c16.sections.2.body: Fixed-size grids are simple, but dense cities produce large buckets while rural areas are empty. Geohashes encode hierarchical subdivisions of longitude and latitude as strings; longer prefixes mean smaller cells. Select precision according to radius and location, then retrieve cells intersecting the search area. Cell boundaries matter: very close businesses can have different prefixes, including around a meridian or the equator. Taking only the center cell misses results. Eight neighbors are a simple pattern for certain coverage conditions, not a universal guarantee when the radius exceeds that group of cells.
c16.sections.3.title: Quadtrees, S2, and index comparison
c16.sections.3.body: A quadtree divides space into four subspaces until buckets are small enough, giving dense areas more subdivisions. An in-memory structure supports radius and k-nearest searches but requires startup construction and coordinated updates. Rolling deployments prevent all servers from building trees simultaneously. S2 maps a sphere’s surface to hierarchical cells and uses Hilbert ordering for indexing; it suits geofence coverage with limits on levels and cell counts. R-trees are another spatial-index family. Geohashes are easier to update, quadtrees adapt to density, and S2 is strong for complex region coverage.
c16.sections.4.title: Sharding and two caches
c16.sections.4.body: Business details can be sharded by business_id for even distribution. The spatial index need not use the same shards; if small enough, read replicas are simpler than complex distribution. A geohash cache stores business IDs per cell, while a business_id cache stores details. Raw GPS coordinates make poor keys because small variations reduce reuse. However, final results still depend on the user’s position and radius, so a cell cache is not an always-correct final list. Business changes must update or invalidate the old cell, new cell, and details to prevent duplicated or missing results.
c16.sections.5.title: Final flow, deployment, and privacy
c16.sections.5.body: The LBS selects cell coverage, requests IDs from caches in parallel, deduplicates candidates, retrieves details in batches, and then calculates distances and sorts results within the radius. For dense cells, candidate limits must preserve result quality or use an appropriate search algorithm. Deploy across availability zones and regions for availability; daily batches match the source’s assumptions but are not required for every product. User location is sensitive data, so define retention and access. Monitor candidates per query, cache misses, percentile latency, and index age to detect hotspots and update delays.
c16.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Geohashes are easy to operate; quadtrees adapt to density.
c16.tradeoffs.0.cost: Geohashes can have dense buckets; quadtrees require builds and complex updates.
c16.tradeoffs.0.when: Use geohashes for radius searches and stable data; use quadtrees for highly skewed distributions or k-nearest searches.
c16.tradeoffs.1.cost: New or relocated businesses do not appear immediately.
c16.tradeoffs.1.when: Choose batching when the product accepts the stated delay.
c16.pitfalls.0: Assuming a shared prefix proves a point is within the radius.
c16.pitfalls.1: Searching only the center cell and missing businesses at boundaries.
c16.pitfalls.2: Adding meters directly to latitude/longitude degrees.

c16.exercise.solution: Choose an appropriate precision and calculate all cells intersecting the search circle; the center and neighboring cells may suffice in this simple pattern, but validate coverage. Retrieve IDs from each cell in parallel, deduplicate them, and then retrieve coordinates and details in batches from caches. Calculate accurate geographic distances and discard candidates outside the radius before sorting and pagination. Cache cell lists for reuse rather than final results keyed by raw coordinates. c17.title: Nearby Friends
c17.summary: Distribute changing locations through WebSocket and pub/sub with TTLs, distance filters, and measured resubscription.
c17.objectives.0: Distinguish moving locations from static business indexes.
c17.objectives.1: Design location flows, pub/sub, and client initialization.
c17.objectives.2: Measure subscription amplification and location updates.
c17.sections.0.title: Scope, estimates, and consistency
c17.sections.0.body: Nearby friends shows friends within a configurable radius along with distance and update timestamps. The source uses straight-line distance, thirty-second refreshes, ten million concurrent users, and an average of four hundred friends. Incoming load is approximately active users divided by refresh interval; outgoing load is then multiplied by active friends. Locations continually change, so a static business index is not directly suitable. The system prioritizes low latency and eventual consistency, accepting some lost updates. Timestamps help users understand stale information, and TTLs remove friends who have been inactive for a long time.
c17.sections.1.title: Shared backend and data layer
c17.sections.1.body: Peer-to-peer is poorly suited to unreliable mobile networks and battery limits. A shared backend receives updates and forwards them to friends authorized to see them. REST APIs manage profiles and relationships; WebSocket servers maintain bidirectional connections. The location cache maps user_id to latitude, longitude, and timestamp with a TTL. The user database stores friendships, while a history database holds location streams for analytics if needed. Redis pub/sub supplies user channels as an example of a lightweight bus. Separate the latest-location cache from history because their read needs, retention, and data-loss tolerances differ.
c17.sections.2.title: Update flow and initialization
c17.sections.2.body: The client sends its location through a WebSocket connection. The server records history, updates the cache and in-memory location, and publishes to the user’s channel. Servers serving friends subscribe to that channel, calculate distances, and only send results satisfying the radius and permissions. When a client first connects, the server retrieves its friend list, subscribes, fetches their cached locations, and sends an initial list. Bootstrap ordering must account for races between snapshots and new events; timestamps or sequences help select the latest update. The socket API also supports subscription and unsubscription when friend status or relationships change.
c17.sections.3.title: Scaling connections, caches, and pub/sub
c17.sections.3.body: REST servers are easy to replicate; WebSocket servers need draining before removal so connections do not suddenly disappear. Location caches can be sharded by user_id, and TTLs limit active entries. Pub/sub is often limited by fanout CPU, not just channel memory; count server deliveries rather than only location-data size. Channel clusters need service discovery and a hash map that socket servers can cache. Consistent hashing reduces channels moved when capacity changes, but subscribers must still resubscribe. Choose low-traffic periods and reconcile from caches to cover some missed updates.
c17.sections.4.title: Changing relationships and popular users
c17.sections.4.body: Adding a friend triggers a new subscription; removing one triggers unsubscription and removal of their location from the display. The server must check permissions against a trusted relationship source instead of accepting every client request blindly. Users with thousands of friends increase subscriptions, distance calculations, and outbound updates; friend limits and hotspot isolation help capacity. Adaptive refresh intervals can save battery when users are stationary, at the cost of lower freshness. Not every pub/sub update is eventually sent to clients because radius filtering occurs after routing to friends’ servers in the basic design.
c17.sections.5.title: Random people, alternatives, and recovery
c17.sections.5.body: A nearby non-friend feature can use geohash channels: clients follow their current cell and neighboring cells so boundaries do not lose candidates. This introduces subscription changes whenever a cell changes and different location-sharing permissions. Erlang is an implementation alternative using many lightweight processes for connections and message passing, but the team needs operational expertise. Redis pub/sub does not provide history replay in the basic model, so after reconnecting, fetch current locations from caches and rebuild subscriptions. History retention and sharing consent require separate product decisions rather than following automatically from using a cache.
c17.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Fast refreshes make distances appear fresher.
c17.tradeoffs.0.cost: There is more radio activity, writing, and update fanout.
c17.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose intervals according to movement speed and experience requirements.
c17.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Pub/sub provides fast distribution without storing every event.
c17.tradeoffs.1.cost: Disconnected subscribers cannot replay all updates.
c17.tradeoffs.1.when: Pub/sub suits cases where the latest location is enough and occasional loss is acceptable.
c17.pitfalls.0: Calculating capacity only from cache memory without fanout CPU.
c17.pitfalls.1: Treating a TTL as sharing permission or a history-retention policy.
c17.pitfalls.2: Assuming consistent hashing removes the need to resubscribe.

With 40 active friends, the simple fanout bound is about 13.33 million subscription deliveries/s before optimizing multiple friends on the same server. Subscriber WebSocket servers check distance and permissions; only the nearby subset is forwarded to clients. A user_id location cache with TTL holds the latest state, history receives asynchronous writes, and channels are distributed using a hash map. When a pub/sub node is added, subscribers perform a handoff and retrieve a cache snapshot to repair missed events.

c18.title: Google Maps
c18.summary: Separate visual maps, road graphs, and location streams for fast, relevant navigation.
c18.objectives.0: Explain visual tiles and hierarchical routing
c18.objectives.1: Calculate the impact of location batching
c18.sections.0.title: Scope, coordinates, and estimation
c18.sections.0.body: Start with location updates, navigation including ETA, and map rendering; business search and multi-stop trips can be extensions. Latitude and longitude identify positions on Earth, while projections transform its surface into a plane that always contains distortion. Web Mercator is suitable for displaying tiles, but distances on the image are no substitute for geographic calculations. Estimate active sessions, sampling frequency, tile sizes, and peak demand separately. Accurate directions, smooth display, battery life, and users' data allowances matter as much as server capacity.
c18.sections.1.title: Geocoding, geohashes, and road graphs
c18.sections.1.body: Geocoding converts addresses into coordinates; reverse geocoding works in the opposite direction. Results can be ambiguous, so quality and partial matches need to reach the route planner. Geohashes provide hierarchical area identifiers and help select spatial data, but neighbors at area boundaries still need checking. For routing, intersections become nodes and roads become directed edges with travel-mode restrictions. Dijkstra or A* operates on this graph. Split the graph into routing tiles with cross-boundary connections, then use different detail levels so long trips do not load the entire world graph.
c18.sections.2.title: Location service and storage model
c18.sections.2.body: Clients sample positions every few seconds but send multiple samples together. Batching reduces request counts and radio overhead, rather than the number of points eventually processed. The payload must carry each sample's coordinates and timestamp so delayed delivery does not change event time. Write-heavy storage can be partitioned by user in time order, with time buckets to limit partition growth. Event streams pass through a queue to traffic analysis. Retention, access, and location precision must be defined; an old position does not automatically represent the user's current state.
c18.sections.3.title: Rendering and tile distribution
c18.sections.3.body: World images are preprocessed at multiple zoom levels, stored as objects, and served through a CDN. In a quadtree model, each zoom increment multiplies the tile count by four; clients fetch only the viewport and a small area ahead along the journey. Visual tiles differ from routing tiles even though both represent areas. Raster tiles are straightforward to display, while vector tiles save transfer and enable client-side styling at a rendering cost. Clients can calculate tile URLs or use an API; the first choice reduces requests but commits to format compatibility. Tile versions and cache invalidation are needed when roads change.
c18.sections.4.title: Route planner, ETA, and data updates
c18.sections.4.body: An offline pipeline converts raw road data into compressed adjacency lists in object storage, with caching for frequently read tiles. The navigation service calls geocoding, pathfinding, ETA prediction, and then a ranker that applies preferences such as avoiding tolls. The shortest route by distance is not necessarily the fastest by time; edge weights must account for travel modes, prohibited turns, and traffic. An updater refreshes graph versions and predictions asynchronously. Separate the read-heavy geocoding model, write-heavy location history, and tile objects so each can scale according to its access pattern.
c18.sections.5.title: Adaptive ETA and delivery protocols
c18.sections.5.body: When an accident occurs, an index from tiles to navigation sessions helps identify affected users without scanning the entire population. Hierarchical area representations can shrink the index, but coarse coverage produces additional candidates that must be checked against actual routes. Recalculate only when the ETA change is meaningful enough to avoid sending constantly changing routes to clients. WebSocket supports bidirectional updates, while SSE suits server-to-client streams. Disconnected sessions must resume with the latest route version. Multi-stop navigation adds visit-order optimization, making its scope different from finding a single path.
c18.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Vectors reduce transfer and support style changes.
c18.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose vectors for capable devices and varied display styles.
c18.tradeoffs.1.when: Match the choice to freshness needs and the battery budget.
c18.pitfalls.0: Visual tiles do not contain the complete navigation graph.
c18.pitfalls.1: Batching does not reduce the number of GPS points.
c18.pitfalls.2: A hierarchical area covering an accident does not prove that a user's route crosses it.

c19.title: Distributed Message Queue
c19.summary: Build a partitioned log with replay, replication, and explicit boundaries for delivery guarantees.
c19.objectives.0: Map topics, partitions, and consumer groups
c19.sections.0.title: Scope and messaging models
c19.sections.0.body: A queue separates producers from consumers so they can grow and fail independently. Point-to-point messaging assigns work to one recipient, while publish-subscribe gives each subscriber group its own view of events. This chapter chooses a log with retention and replay rather than immediate deletion after consumption. Define message sizes, retention periods, latency targets, and ordering requirements before selecting technology. Ordering guarantees apply within partitions; global ordering requires coordination that can reduce parallelism. Queues absorb temporary disruptions but do not solve the problem of consumers that are permanently slower than producers.
c19.sections.1.title: Topics, brokers, and consumer groups
c19.sections.1.body: A topic is split into partitions across brokers. A key such as account_id selects the partition so events for the same account remain ordered. An offset identifies an event's position within one partition and is not a global ID. Each consumer group has its own offsets, allowing audit and business processing to read the same events without duplicating payloads in the log. Within a group, one partition is assigned to one consumer to preserve order. Adding more consumers than partitions does not increase parallelism. Topic metadata, replica mappings, and consumption state need consistent storage with functions distinct from payload storage.
c19.sections.2.title: WAL, message structure, and batching
c19.sections.2.body: An append-only log benefits from sequential disk access. Each partition consists of segments; only the active segment receives appends, while old segments can be deleted according to retention or archived. Messages carry a key, value, topic, partition, offset, timestamp, size, and checksum. Compatible schemas reduce conversion and copying between components; keys may repeat. Producers, brokers, and consumers batch messages to share round-trip and I/O costs. Larger batches improve throughput but add waiting time. Maximum sizes and flush timeouts must together bound latency when traffic is low.
c19.sections.3.title: Producer and consumer flows and rebalancing
c19.sections.3.body: Producers fetch leader metadata and send directly to the destination broker, avoiding an extra routing hop. Per-partition buffers enable efficient batching. Consumers pull data starting at an offset, controlling their own rate; long polling reduces empty requests. The group coordinator monitors heartbeats and schedules rebalancing when members or partitions change. New owners continue from committed offsets, rather than the old consumer's in-memory position. Rebalancing must prevent two active owners from changing the same state. The coordination service for discovery and elections differs from the consumer group coordinator, although both support cluster management.
c19.sections.4.title: Replication, ISR, and capacity changes
c19.sections.4.body: Each partition has a leader and followers on different brokers. Followers catch up with the leader's log; sufficiently current replicas form the in-sync replicas, or ISR. No-wait acknowledgment, leader acknowledgment, and acknowledgment from all ISR offer different combinations of latency and durability. A minimum ISR must restrict writes when too few replicas remain; acknowledging all ISR alone does not guarantee multiple copies. When a new broker joins, copy data before removing old replicas. Additional partitions trigger assignment changes and may alter key mappings. Decommissioned partitions remain readable until retention ends, so reducing capacity is more than deleting files.
c19.sections.5.title: Semantics and advanced features
c19.sections.5.body: Committing offsets before processing effects produces at-most-once behavior with a risk of lost work. Committing afterward produces at-least-once behavior with possible repetition after a crash. Exactly-once effects require a transaction connecting output and offsets, or an idempotent sink with sufficiently long deduplication; broker configuration does not automatically protect external APIs. Broker-side tag filtering reduces transfer but adds evaluation cost. Delayed messages can be stored temporarily with a timer or timing wheel, then moved into the log when due. Retry topics, dead-letter handling, interoperable protocols, and historical archives complete system operations.
c19.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Acknowledgment from all ISR protects data when the leader fails.
c19.tradeoffs.0.cost: Slow replicas increase latency or stop writes.
c19.tradeoffs.0.when: Use a minimum ISR for important events.
c19.tradeoffs.1.when: Use long polling for varying workloads.
c19.pitfalls.0: Multiple partitions do not provide global ordering.
c19.pitfalls.1: Consumers beyond the partition count may sit idle.
c19.pitfalls.2: Broker exactly-once guarantees do not cover every external effect.

c19.exercise.solution: Only six consumers are active, giving a capacity of 12,000 events/second and growing the backlog by 6,000 every second. Eight partitions activate eight consumers, but the new capacity is still only 16,000. At least nine consumers and partitions are needed to match traffic, with additional headroom for failures. Plan key migration to preserve order, monitor lag, and prevent the backlog from exceeding retention.

c20.title: Metrics Monitoring and Alerting System
c20.summary: Control time-series cardinality, retention, and an alert pipeline that tolerates disruptions.
c20.objectives.0: Distinguish metrics from logs and tracing
c20.objectives.1: Calculate the series explosion caused by labels
c20.objectives.2: Design tiered retention and alert deduplication
c20.sections.0.title: Scope, five components, and scale
c20.sections.0.body: Operational monitoring observes CPU, memory, disk space, request rates, and queue lengths. Logs and distributed tracing have different data shapes and purposes, so they are not automatically in scope. The system comprises collection, transmission, storage, alerting, and visualization. Machine count multiplied by metrics per machine gives an initial series estimate, but label variations can change it dramatically. Define sampling intervals, retention, query delays, and notification channels. During incidents, dashboard reads increase precisely when infrastructure is under stress; this demand must be considered alongside routine writes.
c20.sections.1.title: Time series and label cardinality
c20.sections.1.body: A series is identified by its metric name and label combination, and then contains timestamp-value pairs. Region and service labels help aggregation, whereas user_id or request_id can create millions of uncontrolled series. Counters, gauges, and histograms require different query interpretations; averaging raw counters usually does not answer a request-rate question. A time-series database provides indexes and compression suited to these patterns. Do not choose a database solely from benchmark numbers in notes; profile actual label distributions, ingestion, incident queries, and retention. Heavy writes and sporadic reads need capacity protection.
c20.sections.2.title: Pull, push, discovery, and ownership
c20.sections.2.body: The pull model retrieves metric endpoints through service discovery; a failed scrape also becomes a signal of target health. Collectors must divide target ownership to avoid accidentally collecting the same series. Consistent hashing can help divide ownership when collectors are added. Push uses agents that send data and can aggregate it beforehand, fitting short-lived jobs or networks that are difficult to reach. However, senders need authentication and collectors need backpressure. Combining both is often useful. Transport is not determined solely by push or pull: both can use HTTP, so do not assume push always uses UDP.
c20.sections.3.title: Pipeline, aggregation, and queries
c20.sections.3.body: A durable queue between collectors and storage absorbs database disruptions and separates collection scaling from processing scaling. Partitioning by series or labels must preserve load distribution; one popular metric name can become a hotspot. Agent-side aggregation reduces transfer, stream-processor aggregation reduces writes, and query-time aggregation preserves raw data but increases read costs. A query service unifies dashboard and alert access and can add a cache with freshness rules. If the database and plugins already suffice, this extra layer is optional. Prioritize critical metrics during overload so monitoring failures themselves remain visible.
c20.sections.4.title: Storage, compression, and downsampling
c20.sections.4.body: Regular timestamps can be compressed using delta or delta-of-delta encoding, and similar values also offer compression opportunities. Keep new data at high resolution, then use minute and hourly rollups as it ages. Explain whether retention phases overlap; the lab example uses seven days of raw data, minute resolution from day eight through day thirty, and hourly resolution through day 365. Averages alone can hide spikes; preserve count, sum, min, and max when questions require all of them. Cold storage lowers costs but slows older investigations and requires a recovery plan.
c20.sections.5.title: Alerting, state, and visualization
c20.sections.5.body: An evaluator runs rules periodically through the query service, including the duration a condition must persist before an alert fires. The alert manager groups, filters, and deduplicates events so one disruption does not flood users with notifications. Alert state is stored durably and events pass to a queue for at-least-once delivery, so receiving channels must handle duplicates too. Access to rule changes needs restrictions and auditing. Dashboards display metrics and alerts with clear units and time ranges. Solutions such as Grafana and ready-made alert components can reduce development costs; monitor the evaluator, queue, and channel delivery success as well.
c20.tradeoffs.0.choice: Aggregation before storage versus at query time
c20.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Early aggregation reduces writes and storage.
c20.tradeoffs.0.cost: Raw details are lost once combined.
c20.tradeoffs.0.when: Preserve sufficient statistics and short-term raw data for investigations.
c20.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Pull simplifies endpoint inspection and target checks.
c20.tradeoffs.1.cost: Collectors must be able to reach targets.
c20.tradeoffs.1.when: Push is useful for short-lived jobs and network boundaries.
c20.pitfalls.0: A request_id label can cause a series explosion.
c20.pitfalls.1: Rollup averages can erase evidence of spikes.
c20.pitfalls.2: An alert queue does not guarantee that humans receive only one notification.

c20.exercise.hints.1: Preserve max as well as average.
c20.exercise.solution: Seven days of raw data produces 12.096 billion points. Days 8–30 produce 6.624 billion minute rollups, and days 31–365 produce 1.608 billion hourly rollups. Rollups carry sum and count for weighted averages plus min/max for spikes, so their sizes differ from raw points. Use compression, hot/cold separation, and cardinality limits. Spike alerts are still evaluated from high-resolution data before downsampling.

c21.title: Ad Click Event Aggregation
c21.summary: Aggregate clicks using event time, deduplication, checkpoints, and auditable reconciliation.
c21.objectives.0: Design aggregation and filtered top-N results
c21.sections.0.title: Scope, APIs, and estimation
c21.sections.0.body: The system answers click counts for an ad over a time range and lists the top-N ads within a particular window. Country, user, or IP filters need to be defined together with query cost limits. A reporting latency of several minutes differs from real-time bidding decisions, which have much shorter deadlines. Estimate daily events, peak factors, record sizes, and growth before deciding partition counts. Accuracy matters because results can affect billing. APIs must explain inclusive or exclusive time boundaries, time zones, result freshness, and whether figures are provisional or finalized after corrections.
c21.sections.1.title: Raw data, aggregates, and the processing DAG
c21.sections.1.body: Raw events carry event_id, ad_id, click time, user, IP, and country. Aggregates store counts by ad, minute, and filter dimension; top-N is a separate view. Raw data is retained for audits and backfills, while views provide fast queries. An event log separates ingestion from the map, aggregate, and reduce DAG. Map validates and groups data, aggregate counts by key, and reduce combines results, including a top-N heap. Dimension preaggregation follows the star-schema pattern, but many filter combinations multiply buckets. Columnar storage in object storage or an OLAP database is an alternative for large-scale analysis.
c21.sections.2.title: Streaming, batches, and event time
c21.sections.2.body: Streaming continuously processes unbounded input; batch processing recalculates a bounded dataset. Lambda uses separate batch and stream paths, while Kappa uses the same processing engine for live data and replay. Replay should use separate capacity to avoid disrupting new reports. Event time indicates when a click occurred, while processing time indicates when the server processes it. Event time better fits window attribution, but client timestamps can be wrong. Validate time ranges, retain reception time, and define correction policies so neither lateness nor manipulation directly becomes a billing result.
c21.sections.3.title: Windows, watermarks, and deduplication
c21.sections.3.body: Tumbling windows do not overlap, hopping windows use a fixed step, sliding windows follow a shifting range, and sessions depend on inactivity gaps. Per-minute counts use tumbling windows, while top-N over several minutes can use sliding windows. A watermark estimates event-time progress rather than guaranteeing that all older events have arrived. Allowed lateness and a correction path determine how late events are handled. Deduplicating event_id handles client resends; storing offsets alone does not solve every duplication problem. Transactions linking output and offsets, or idempotent writes of versioned window results, prevent a crash after output from adding counts twice.
c21.sections.4.title: Scale, hotspots, and fault tolerance
c21.sections.4.body: Queues, aggregation workers, and databases can scale independently. Enough partitions enable consumer-group parallelism, but a very popular ad can make one key dominate. Split hot keys into subkeys and combine partial counts using global-local aggregation; adding workers without splitting the key does not fix the bottleneck. In-memory state such as counts and top-N heaps needs checkpoints together with input positions. Recovery loads a consistent snapshot and replays from the corresponding offsets. Rebalancing, partition-count changes, and backfills must preserve ownership boundaries so two workers do not publish results that overwrite each other.
c21.sections.5.title: Monitoring, reconciliation, and alternatives
c21.sections.5.body: Monitor record lag, event age, checkpoint duration, worker resources, sink failures, and differences between input and output counts. A queue log does not delete consumed events, so physical log size does not measure backlog; offset differences are more appropriate. Reconciliation recalculates raw data, compares per-ad and per-window results with the views, and produces identifiable corrections. This also catches logic bugs that server-health checks cannot detect. ClickHouse or Druid can provide OLAP aggregation; assess choices by query dimensions, operating cost, replay, and correction guarantees rather than simply listing products.
c21.tradeoffs.0.benefit: A larger allowance includes more late events.
c21.tradeoffs.0.cost: Finalization is slower and state is retained longer.
c21.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose tolerance according to actual delay distributions and daily corrections.
c21.tradeoffs.1.cost: New dimensions require replay and many buckets.
c21.tradeoffs.1.when: Preaggregate popular filters and preserve raw data for exploration.
c21.pitfalls.0: A watermark does not prove there are no older events.
c21.pitfalls.1: Deduplicating by ad_id removes legitimate clicks.
c21.pitfalls.2: Exactly-once requires explicit transaction and sink boundaries.

c21.exercise.solution: The hot key receives 20,000 events/second, so split it into at least four subkeys, with more than four for headroom. Each worker produces a count per ad_id, subkey, and window. The reducer combines the latest version of each result idempotently rather than repeatedly adding replays. Deduplication still uses event_id; checkpoint state and offsets consistently. Raw-data reconciliation verifies that key splitting does not change the final total.

c22.title: Hotel Reservation System
c22.summary: Protect inventory by room type and date using transactions, idempotency, and concurrency control.
c22.sections.0.title: Scope, capacity, and APIs
c22.sections.0.body: Core features include hotel pages, room-type details, reservations, cancellations, payments, and administration. Prices can change for each date, while overbooking is an explicit business policy, such as up to ten percent above inventory. Do not confuse this policy with overselling caused by race conditions. Occupancy and stay-length estimates yield booking volumes, while conversion funnels yield page traffic that is usually much larger. Hotel and room APIs support administration; reservation APIs provide creation, history, details, and cancellation. A reservation ID or idempotency key links retries to the same operation.
c22.sections.1.title: Initial model and service architecture
c22.sections.1.body: A relational database suits hotel, room, user, and reservation structures, especially because inventory operations need transactions. Individual-room models work for unique properties, but hotels usually sell room types and assign room numbers later. The hotel service provides cacheable metadata, the rate service provides prices by date, and the reservation service handles inventory and booking status. The payment service interacts with payment providers; the management service offers restricted administrative functions. A CDN handles static assets and a gateway provides authentication and request limits. Internal communication can use RPC without turning every table into a separate service.
c22.sections.2.title: Room-type inventory and date ranges
c22.sections.2.body: Inventory is keyed by hotel_id, room_type_id, and date, with total_inventory and total_reserved. Rates by type and date are stored separately so the final price can be captured as a snapshot when booking. A daily job prepares rows for future dates. Multi-night reservations must succeed for every date or fail entirely; the checkout night is not an occupied night. Effective capacity is floor(inventory × overbooking factor), with defined rounding. Row counts can be estimated from hotels, types, and the date horizon. Old history can be archived, but changes and cancellation audits must remain traceable.
c22.sections.3.title: Idempotency and concurrency control
c22.sections.3.body: Two distinct problems occur when a user clicks twice and when two users book the last inventory. A unique idempotency key resolves the first retry problem, while inventory updates require concurrency control. Pessimistic locking locks rows before checking and updating, suiting high contention but increasing queues and deadlock risk. Optimistic locking reads a version and updates only if the version remains the same; use version equality rather than merely requiring a larger new version. Constraints or conditional updates protect capacity limits. All nightly rows must be updated in one transaction with a consistent locking order.
c22.sections.4.title: Scalability, caches, and shards
c22.sections.4.body: Stateless services can be replicated, but databases need a query-based strategy. Sharding by hotel_id keeps one hotel's inventory together and limits cross-shard transactions. A Redis cache for availability searches reduces reads; CDC can refresh the cache after database changes. Caches may lag, so an available display is not a promise that a reservation will succeed. Final decisions always check authoritative inventory within a transaction. TTL removes past dates and cache versions help invalidation. Read replicas are useful for metadata or searches, but stale reads must not drive mutations without revalidation.
c22.sections.5.title: Payment and service consistency
c22.sections.5.body: Combining reservations and inventory within one database boundary enables ACID without cross-service protocols. If separated, two-phase commit provides atomicity at the cost of blocking and coordinator dependency; a saga provides a sequence of local transactions with eventually consistent compensation. Payments need a state machine such as pending, confirmed, cancelled, and refunded, plus reconciliation for ambiguous responses. Inventory holds need expiration and idempotent release. Compensation is not a magical undo: refunds can fail or arrive late. Choose service boundaries according to organizational needs and scale while maintaining capacity invariants and a clear change history.
c22.tradeoffs.0.benefit: Optimistic locking avoids holding locks when contention is low.
c22.tradeoffs.0.cost: High contention causes retries and wasted work.
c22.tradeoffs.0.when: Choose according to contention per hotel, not just global QPS.
c22.tradeoffs.1.choice: Availability cache versus direct database access
c22.tradeoffs.1.benefit: Caching speeds up searches and reduces reads.
c22.tradeoffs.1.cost: The UI may show inventory that has already sold out.
c22.tradeoffs.1.when: Revalidate bookings in the authoritative database.
c22.pitfalls.0: An idempotency key does not replace inventory locking.
c22.pitfalls.1: The checkout date is not a night that needs booking.
c22.pitfalls.2: Intentional overbooking still has a transactional limit.

c22.exercise.solution: The bottleneck is the second night with one room, so each two-room request must be rejected before commit. Retrying with the same idempotency key must not add a reservation. If the UI uses a cache, return an availability conflict together with refreshed search results.

c23.title: Distributed Email Service
c23.summary: Separate metadata, attachments, delivery queues, and search indexes for reliable mailboxes.
c23.objectives.0: Explain protocols and mail flows between domains
c23.sections.0.title: Scope, protocols, and estimation
c23.sections.0.body: Features include sending, receiving, listing folders, reading, filtering, searching, attachments, and spam checks. SMTP transfers messages between servers; MX DNS records help locate a domain's destination. IMAP synchronizes server mailboxes, while POP retrieves messages with configurable storage policies, so deletion is not mandatory in every installation. Webmail uses HTTPS for rich operations. MIME carries attachments and base64 encoding increases transfer sizes. Estimate sending volumes, recipient copy counts, metadata, and attachments separately. Storage reliability and feature extensibility usually matter more than optimizing a single simple request.
c23.sections.1.title: From traditional servers to distributed services
c23.sections.1.body: Traditional servers may store each email as a local file, but a single disk limits capacity and becomes a failure point. A distributed design separates the web API, real-time gateway, metadata store, attachment object storage, new-message cache, and search store. Message creation, folder listing, paginated message listing, and message-detail endpoints form the client contract. Attachments are referenced as objects rather than repeatedly passed through queues. WebSocket provides new-message notifications, with polling fallback if necessary. Notifications accelerate the UI; offline users still obtain authoritative data through the API when they return.
c23.sections.2.title: Outbound, inbound, and retry flows
c23.sections.2.body: Outbound processing validates addresses, sizes, and sending policies before placing messages in a durable queue. Workers check spam or viruses and send SMTP to destinations; local domains can use an internal path with equivalent checks. The Sent folder records system acceptance, while delivery status separately indicates the sending result. Temporary disruptions are rescheduled with exponential backoff; permanent failures produce bounces. Inbound processing applies acceptance policies, separates attachments, and stores metadata before updating caches, indexes, and real-time gateways. Monitor the oldest message's age, not just queue length, and isolate slow domains so they do not block all recipients.
c23.sections.3.title: Metadata, folders, and consistency
c23.sections.3.body: Mailbox operations are generally isolated to one user, making user_id a natural partition key. Folders, time-ordered messages, attachment references, and read/unread state are arranged according to queries. A wide-column database may require denormalized tables for unread queries; updates across representations need consistency and recovery rules. Conversation threads can be built from Message-ID, In-Reply-To, and References. Headers are read frequently, while bodies are larger and read less often, so they can use different caches. Losing email is unacceptable; strong mutation consistency may sacrifice temporary availability during network partitions, with tested backups and restores.
c23.sections.4.title: Deliverability and reputation protection
c23.sections.4.body: A successful SMTP handoff does not prove a message reached the inbox. Sender reputation, complaints, traffic patterns, and domain authentication affect classification. Separate important traffic from marketing, restrict abusive accounts, monitor bounces and complaints, and build reputation gradually according to destination providers. SPF and DKIM support authentication, complemented by domain policies such as DMARC. A dedicated IP does not guarantee deliverability; volume and operations determine its benefits. Antispam also applies inbound through content, malware, and phishing checks. Per-destination throttling policies and feedback loops must be part of delivery operations, rather than features added only after queues grow.
c23.sections.5.title: Search, scale, availability, and optimizations
c23.sections.5.body: Email search is limited to the user's mailbox and supports sender, subject, date, and unread filters, with ordering often based on time. Change events pass asynchronously to an Elasticsearch index or a custom engine; queries must explain index lag so users understand why new messages may not appear yet. Custom LSM-based search optimizes sequential writes but adds engineering and compaction costs. Partitioning by user_id simplifies isolation and must accommodate very large mailboxes. Multi-datacenter replication, leader-follower failover, access security, personal-data protection, incremental backups, and attachment deduplication complete the design; deduplication must still preserve object authorization.
