c24.sections.0.body: Block storage exposes raw blocks; file storage adds names and directories; object storage provides buckets, keys, payloads, and metadata through an API. Slashes in a key form a prefix, not a physical directory. The exercise covers buckets, uploads, downloads, object listings, and versions. A 100 PB capacity target requires estimates of object-size distribution, metadata-record counts, IOPS, and recovery headroom. Durability means data remains stored, whereas availability means the service can be accessed. They require different measurements and do not automatically guarantee each other.
c24.sections.1.body: A load balancer routes requests to a stateless API. The API checks identity and permissions through IAM before accessing a bucket. During upload, the data store saves the payload and returns an object ID; metadata then links the bucket, key, version, and that ID. During download, metadata lookup finds the ID, and the routing service retrieves contents from a data node. This separation lets metadata and bytes scale independently. Failure after payload storage but before metadata publication creates an orphan, so success and cleanup need explicit rules.
c24.sections.2.body: The placement service maintains a map of nodes, disk capacities, and heartbeat status using consensus-based replication. The routing service uses that map to select an object's storage group. The primary writes and replicates before acknowledging success according to the durability policy. Putting each small object in a separate file wastes blocks and inodes. Instead, combine objects in large append-only files with a local index containing object ID, file name, offset, and length. SQLite or another local store avoids network trips during lookup. Index updates must follow byte persistence with a clear recovery procedure.
c24.sections.3.body: Three copies require three times the logical capacity, but a read can use one healthy copy. Erasure coding with 8+4 stores eight data fragments and four parity fragments, producing a capacity multiplier of 1.5. Up to four missing fragments can still be reconstructed, requiring additional networking and computation. Spread fragments or replicas across racks and zones to avoid correlated failures. Per-object and per-fragment checksums detect silent corruption, while scrubbing and repair correct it. Independent disk probabilities are insufficient to promise a number of nines: software bugs, repair time, and shared failures also determine the outcome.
c24.sections.4.body: Minimum metadata includes the bucket, key, object ID, size, version, and logical location. Hashing the bucket and key spreads direct lookups, but prefix listing must contact many shards. A coordinator fetches sorted results from each shard and merges them; cursor pagination must retain progress for every shard to avoid missing or repeated results. A separate listing index partitioned by bucket can accelerate listings at the cost of synchronization and the risk of a popular bucket becoming a hotspot. Partition choices should follow actual query patterns, not object counts alone. Do not use a global offset as if all data lived in one database.
c24.sections.5.body: Replacing a key creates a new immutable object and a new version record. A delete marker hides the latest version without immediately deleting history, so retention rules remain important. For large files, the client starts a multipart session, obtains an upload ID, and sends numbered parts in parallel. Completion verifies all parts and publishes final object metadata; failed parts can be retried without resending the whole file. An ETag is an implementation-dependent identifier and is not always an object's MD5 checksum. Parallelism speeds up transfer until client bandwidth, server bandwidth, or part count becomes the bottleneck.
c24.sections.6.body: Delete markers, abandoned multipart sessions, and uploads without metadata leave bytes that may not yet be safe to discard. A collector checks retention, version references, and session age before marking data reclaimable. In a combined file, compaction copies live objects to a new file and atomically switches mappings; the old file is deleted only once readers and replicas are safe. Corrupt objects should be restored from redundancy before the final copy is discarded. Cleanup includes every replica or parity fragment. Run it incrementally so compaction and repair I/O do not exhaust capacity on the user path.
c25.sections.0.body: A monthly tournament leaderboard needs the top ten, a user's rank, and optionally four neighbors on either side. First define what a score means, who may increase it, and tie rules. For five million daily players and ten matches per player, calculate daily events and divide by 86,400 seconds, then add a peak factor. Do not confuse registered players with concurrent connections. The source mixes several DAU figures in its estimates, so the exercise uses explicit, adjustable assumptions. A real-time target also needs a lag bound, not merely the label fast.
c25.sections.1.body: The score-update endpoint must be called by a game server that has validated a win, not a client free to change points. Include a tournament ID and unique match ID so redelivering a result does not increase the score twice. The leaderboard service updates scores, while read APIs provide top-K and user rank. A queue helps when rewards or analytics services also need results, but adds consumption lag. A durable match-results table supplies reconstruction data if the cache is lost. Player profiles are stored separately; caching top-player profiles reduces repeated queries when many users open the same list.
c25.sections.2.body: A relational database is sufficient for small tournaments: records contain tournament, user, and score, with a unique tournament-user key. A score index helps fetch top-K, but a middle-ranked user's rank still requires counting participants with higher scores. A Redis sorted set stores unique members and an ordered index, commonly using a hash and skip list. ZINCRBY increases a score, range retrieves a list, and rank finds a position at logarithmic cost. This convenience does not make Redis automatically durable. Persistence, replicas, and a match-results log are needed to choose a recovery strategy and measure acceptable event loss.
c25.sections.3.body: A sorted-set position has a single order, whereas two equal-scoring players may need to share a business rank. For competition rank, rank is one plus the number of players with higher scores; for dense rank, count distinct higher scores. If ties must be broken, consistently define a win-time or ID rule. Neighbors come from a positional range around a player, with handling for the beginning and end boundaries. A new set per tournament separates seasons; old seasons are archived. Score-representation limits and structural overhead should be measured rather than assumed to equal ID length plus a small integer.
c25.sections.4.body: An API gateway and serverless functions can run endpoints without managing all application-server capacity. Managed Redis and profile databases also reduce provisioning, backup, and failover work, but users remain responsible for data design, permissions, and idempotency. Self-management gives control over configuration and tuning at a higher on-call cost. Consider cold starts, database connections, concurrency limits, and per-call costs before choosing. A benchmark mixing updates and rank queries is more useful than a generic throughput figure. Memory headroom is needed for persistence and snapshot processes, not just the main dataset.
c25.sections.5.body: Range sharding by score lets top-K begin at the highest-score shard. Global rank can add the number of players in higher ranges to local rank, but score changes must move members correctly. Popular ranges may become hotspots, and counters need consistency. Hash sharding distributes players more evenly; top-K must fetch candidates from every shard and merge them. Global rank needs the count of higher scores on every shard, not just local ZRANK. Redis Cluster partitions keys, so one large sorted-set key does not automatically split across machines. Splitting members requires application design.
c25.sections.6.body: NoSQL with a tournament partition key and score sort key supports ordering within a partition, but the entire active season may become a hotspot. Write sharding adds a partition number derived from user ID; top-K reads then become scatter-gather. More partitions make write distribution easier but increase candidate collection. Exact rank is not free; a percentile based on periodic distributions can be an alternative if the product allows approximation. During a Redis outage, replay durable match results with deduplication, then switch to the verified dataset. Tests must ensure scores, ties, and event ordering still follow season rules.
c26.sections.0.body: A payment backend receives customer money for merchants through pay-in and sends merchant balances through pay-out. The initial scope uses one currency and an external PSP, so the system does not build a card network itself. One million transactions per day averages approximately 11.6 per second; peaks and payment orders per checkout still need estimation. The main challenge is not that throughput figure but correct records when some systems fail. Define pending, successful, and terminally failed statuses, along with how users check results. Reconciliation is a core function because communication with external parties is not atomic.
c26.sections.1.body: The payment service saves a checkout event and creates one or more payment orders. An executor processes each order through the PSP using a stable payment order ID. POST payments creates the request, while GET by ID returns stored status. The model separates checkout from payment orders and stores amount, currency, PSP token, status, and ledger and wallet progress. Use integer minor units or an exact decimal; a string API representation avoids floating-point rounding but still needs validation. A unique constraint protects the order ID. Status transitions must follow a state machine rather than freely changing booleans.
c26.sections.2.body: The ledger stores paired entries whose signed total is zero for each transaction, making value flows traceable. Debit and credit are accounting concepts whose effect depends on account type, not universal synonyms for decreasing and increasing a balance. The wallet is a merchant-balance projection that must match the ledger and must not recognize money twice. Pay-out moves funds to a merchant's account, with separate available-balance checks, settlement status, and bookkeeping. A successful customer payment does not always mean funds have settled or are immediately withdrawable. Corrections use new traceable entries instead of deleting old history.
c26.sections.3.body: The backend registers the order with the PSP and stores a token before directing the user to a PSP-hosted payment page. Card data goes directly to that provider; the application stores necessary references rather than raw card numbers. The browser redirect helps the user experience but is not final proof of payment success. The backend validates PSP webhooks, links them to orders, and processes events idempotently. Webhook order may change, or events may be redelivered. If the PSP requires additional checks such as user authentication or risk review, show pending and use controlled polling when webhooks are unavailable.
c26.sections.4.body: Synchronous HTTP is simple, but a PSP-wallet-ledger chain adds latency and spreads failures. Queues provide buffering and let multiple subscribers record side effects, at the cost of lag and duplicate delivery. A transactional outbox links database changes to events that must be sent. Retries with backoff and jitter handle transient failures; terminal errors go to a dead-letter queue for investigation. Once-only effects require retries to achieve at-least-once behavior and deduplication at every receiver. An idempotency key must remain stable for the same payment intent and be bound to its payload; a timeout does not prove the PSP has not charged. Do not retry with a new key because the first response was lost.
c26.sections.5.body: A scheduled process compares PSP settlement reports with internal orders, then compares ledger and wallet. Classify differences into known automatic cases, cases requiring human action, and unclassified cases. Keep evidence, correction reasons, and investigation outcomes for auditing. A background worker checks old orders still executing and resumes unfinished side effects. Primary reads or consistency-guaranteed reads are needed for balance decisions; a lagging replica may display stale data. A local ACID transaction does not make the PSP and every service one global transaction. Reconciliation complements duplicate prevention rather than replacing it.
c26.sections.6.body: Use TLS, service authentication, webhook-integrity verification, and separate secret management. Tokenization and hosted payment pages reduce card-data exposure; compliance requirements still depend on the integration and environment. Restrict correction operations, protect APIs with rate limiting, and audit sensitive changes. Backups, replication, and restore exercises protect transaction history. Monitoring should highlight long-pending payments, retries, settlement discrepancies, and unbalanced ledgers. Design extensions may include different currencies, local methods, cash payments, and device wallets, with amount rules and lifecycles defined for each method.
c27.sections.0.body: A wallet moves balances between two internal accounts without covering currency conversion. The exercise target of one million transfers per second means at least two account changes per transfer. Node capacity must be measured with actual transactions, persistence, and replication; generic database TPS figures are only initial assumptions. POST balance_transfer accepts source and destination accounts, an exact amount, currency, and transaction ID for idempotency. Available balance and sender identity are validated before accepting a transfer. Reliability and availability need separate definitions; reproducibility adds the requirement to prove historical balances through replay rather than merely storing the latest value.
c27.sections.1.body: A Redis map from account to balance can be partitioned by account-ID hash, while shard configuration lives in a highly available service. A stateless API can scale horizontally, but changes to two accounts on different shards are not yet atomic, and memory alone provides no durable history. Partitioned relational databases with two-phase commit ask every participant to prepare, then commit if all agree. Participants may hold locks while a decision is unavailable. The coordinator needs a durable log and recovery; its failure does not always lose data but can leave transactions blocked. Measure contention and cross-shard paths before choosing a protocol.
c27.sections.2.body: TCC divides a transfer into local transactions that reserve resources, then confirm or cancel. For a wallet, try reduces the sender's available balance or creates a hold; the recipient must not spend nonfinal value. Confirm completes receipt, while cancel releases the hold. A phase-status table records transaction ID, sent steps, responses, decisions, and recovery progress. Every step must be idempotent. A cancel arriving before try needs a tombstone so a late try does not reserve money again. Temporary imbalance must be recorded as in-flight value rather than treated as lost money. A recovered coordinator continues the same durable decision.
c27.sections.3.body: A saga runs local steps sequentially, then compensates successful steps when a later step fails. A transfer debits the sender before crediting the recipient; a failed credit needs an idempotent, retryable refund. Orchestration places the lifecycle in a coordinator, whereas choreography distributes it through event subscribers. Orchestration is easier to trace for wallet flows requiring audit, but needs a good recovery log. Both sagas and TCC can expose intermediate state and do not automatically provide isolation equivalent to a global ACID transaction. Compensation is a new transaction, so cancellation does not erase the fact that the original attempt occurred.
c27.sections.4.body: A command expresses intent such as a transfer and can be rejected; an event expresses an accepted fact. State is a balance projection, while a state machine applies events deterministically. Store external-check results in the facts needed so replay does not repeat I/O or use new random values. Log order is maintained per transaction domain; cross-shard operations still require coordination. Event replay restores a balance at a historical point and compares results across code versions. CQRS separates read projections from the command path. Lagging projections must show a watermark or pending status so users do not assume the displayed balance is always current.
c27.sections.5.body: A local append-only log reduces network trips; mmap maps a file into memory but does not itself guarantee flushing or durability. Caching recent logs and local state such as RocksDB helps the write path. A snapshot saves state together with the exact log offset, allowing recovery to replay only later events. Committed events must be replicated through a consensus group such as Raft before acknowledgement according to the durability contract. A majority of nodes is needed for progress; state and snapshots can be rebuilt if the log is complete. Commands alone may be insufficient because earlier decisions may depend on unrecorded nondeterministic results.
c27.sections.6.body: One Raft group has limited capacity, so accounts are divided among groups. Cross-group transfers use a TCC or saga coordinator that stores the phase before sending steps. Each leader validates a command, produces an event, replicates it, and updates a projection. Projection results are sent back through a reverse proxy or coordinator so clients do not poll continuously. A proxy can batch queries when polling is still needed, but push reduces the time until users learn the outcome. The final design combines local logs, consensus, snapshots, CQRS, and cross-shard transactions. Optimizations must still preserve unique IDs, nonnegative balances, and total value including holds.
c28.sections.0.body: An exchange matches buy and sell orders arriving through brokers. The initial scope supports stocks, new limit orders, and cancellations during trading hours. A limit buy must not pay above its limit; a limit sell must not receive below its limit. The best bid is the highest buy price, and the best ask is the lowest sell price. L1 shows the best prices, L2 depth by level, and L3 order details. One billion orders over 6.5 hours is about 42,735 orders per second, with larger peaks at market opening. Wallet, risk-check, security, and p99 requirements must be defined separately.
c28.sections.1.body: The client gateway receives broker protocols, validates sessions, performs authentication and rate limiting, and forwards minimal messages. The order manager performs risk checks and reserves funds or inventory before an order enters the matching engine. A sequencer assigns numbers so the engine processes the same order on primary and replica. Order creation includes symbol, side, integer-tick price, quantity, and client order ID; cancellation references an open order ID. The execution API returns fills and remaining quantity, not just success or failure. REST can serve general access, while FIX or dedicated protocols support broker integration with different latency needs.
c28.sections.2.body: A product stores instrument rules such as symbol, tick size, and lot; an order expresses intent that may not be immediately fulfilled; an execution is an immutable matching result. An order book consists of sorted price levels with FIFO queues at each level and an order-ID index for cancellation. A doubly linked list helps insert and delete orders already located, but searching for or creating price levels still incurs index-structure costs. Buy matching starts at the cheapest ask not exceeding the limit; sell matching works in reverse. Partial fills reduce both sides' remaining quantities. Canceling a fully filled order cannot undo its previous execution.
c28.sections.3.body: The market-data publisher receives order-book events and executions to create snapshots, depth deltas, and open-high-low-close-volume candles per interval. Executions alone cannot reconstruct the entire resting book because unmatched new orders and cancellations also change it. The data service provides books and candles with sequence watermarks so subscribers recognize gaps. The reporter stores history for audit, settlement, and reporting outside the critical path. Preallocated ring buffers reduce allocations; in-memory candles are limited and history is persisted. Padding can reduce false sharing, but a ring buffer is not automatically lock-free without correct access design and memory ordering.
c28.sections.4.body: Reduce critical-path work and network trips by combining components that need low latency. A shared-memory or mmap event bus can accelerate process communication; files in shared memory still need separate persistence and replication strategies. An application loop pinned to a particular core reduces contention and context switching. A single-writer sequencer provides ordering, while an event log stores facts for replay. Matching must avoid unrecorded local time or randomness. Functional determinism means ordered inputs produce identical outputs; latency determinism means timing variation is controlled. Monitor p99 and p99.99, including garbage-collection and queue effects.
c28.sections.5.body: Stateful replicas can apply the same events, but only a leader with a valid epoch may publish results. Heartbeats and fencing prevent two active matching engines during a partition. Warm standby reduces failover time, while snapshots plus event logs support broader recovery. Define the RTO, data-loss limit, and when an order is acknowledged as durable; asynchronous replication alone does not guarantee zero loss. Raft or another consensus mechanism can preserve decision order at the cost of quorum latency. Test shared bugs, damaged disks, lost servers, and site outages. Replication does not protect against identical logic errors on every replica.
c28.sections.6.body: Price-time priority chooses the best price first, then the earliest order at that price. Validate the next sequence before changing state, and save results for redelivery deduplication. Multicast distribution sends one stream to many subscribers efficiently; UDP needs sequencing, gap detection, and retransmission. Multicast does not guarantee identical arrival times because network paths differ. Colocation reduces network distance but needs explicit access and fairness policies. Separate public gateways from private trading paths, use allowlists, rate limits, and public-data caches. This design teaches software architecture, not investment strategies.

legacy.scaling.challenge: Handle 3,600 req/s with at most 4 web servers, all servers healthy, and no unserved requests.
legacy.scaling.hint: The database must receive at most 500 queries/s. Also check the capacity of 4 × 600 req/s: is this target possible?
legacy.scaling.answer: This target is impossible with at most 4 servers: the web tier can handle only 2,400 req/s, even with 95% caching. Negotiate the constraints: 6 active servers and at least 90% caching on this slider will serve 3,600 req/s.

legacy.scaling.challengeIdle: Apply the constraints, then find the bottleneck. This challenge tests feasibility rather than a score.
legacy.rate.lessonTitle: Choose a limit that suits the traffic pattern.
legacy.rate.challenge: Compare 20 requests arriving around the 10-second boundary. Find an algorithm that accepts at most 10 requests in any 10-second interval.
legacy.rate.hint: Select sliding window log, then run the window boundary scenario. Compare it with fixed window.
legacy.rate.answer: With a limit of 10, sliding log accepts 10 and rejects 10. Fixed window accepts 20 because the counter resets at t=10s. A token bucket with capacity 10 and refill 1/s accepts 10: the 0.2s gap adds only 0.2 tokens.

legacy.hash.challenge: Compare key movement from 3 to 4 nodes, then repeat with 1 and 32 virtual nodes per server.
legacy.hash.hint: Reset the node count to 3 after changing virtual nodes. Measure movement and keys on the busiest node.
legacy.hash.answer: There is no universal percentage for small samples. With an ideal distribution, adding a fourth node takes about 1/4 of the keys. Virtual nodes help balance ownership, but the number of keys moved in any particular experiment can be higher or lower.

legacy.scaling.assumptions: Capacity = min(active servers × 600, 500 / (1 − hit rate)). No queues, writes, retries, or cache costs. The load balancer is assumed to be powerful enough.
legacy.rate.assumptions: One client, one limiter, no race conditions. Auto sends 5 requests together every 1 second of simulation time.
legacy.hash.assumptions: Dark border = owner changed. No replication; key distribution is not traffic distribution. Hot keys can still cause overload.
legacy.scaling.overloadInsight: {bottleneck} is the bottleneck. The system receives {incoming} req/s, but its effective capacity is only {capacity} req/s. {recovery}
legacy.scaling.healthyInsight: All requests are handled. Caching reduces database load to {database} queries/s. The next limit is at {bottleneck}; about {headroom} req/s of headroom remains.
legacy.rate.tokenCaption: The bucket starts full; refill is {refill} tokens/second; each request uses one token.
legacy.rate.fixedCaption: Current window [{start}, {end}) seconds. The quota resets at the window boundary.
legacy.rate.tokenInsight: The bucket stores up to {limit} tokens, allowing bursts even above the refill rate per second. Once empty, quota returns at {refill} tokens/second. Tokens above capacity are not stored.
legacy.rate.fixedInsight: The counter resets every 10 seconds. Two bursts on either side of a window boundary can allow up to {limit} requests in a short time. The per-window limit is still respected.
legacy.rate.slidingInsight: Sliding log counts accepted requests in the last 10 seconds. This prevents surges at window boundaries, at the memory cost of storing timestamps.
legacy.hash.insight: When changing from {before} to {after} nodes, consistent hashing moves {moved} keys; modulo moves {moduloMoved}. {explanation} Virtual nodes help balance ownership but do not guarantee perfect distribution in small samples.
legacy.rate.challengeResult: Result for {algorithm}: {accepted} accepted, {rejected} rejected. Change the algorithm and repeat the scenario.
legacy.hash.challengeResult: Last change: {before} to {after} nodes, {vnodes} virtual nodes per server. Compare the two movement counts in the results panel.
legacy.scaling.lessonIntro: A load balancer distributes requests to stateless web servers. Caching reduces database reads but does not replace primary storage. Adding servers helps only when the web tier is the bottleneck.
legacy.scaling.horizontalLesson: {label} capacity and redundancy increase; sessions must be accessible across servers.
legacy.scaling.cacheLesson: {label} faster access at the cost of memory, invalidation, and stale-data risk. The hit rate in this lab is an input rather than a simulated eviction result.
legacy.scaling.failureLesson: {label} one failed server reduces capacity. Redundancy without spare capacity may be insufficient.
legacy.scaling.lessonAssumptions: Requests are assumed to be read-only and evenly distributed. Each server handles 600 req/s and the database 500 queries/s. Capacity follows {formula}. This model does not account for latency, queues, cache stampedes, failover delay, or infrastructure costs.
legacy.rate.lessonIntro: Token bucket allows bursts up to the token capacity. Fixed window is easy to calculate, but the boundary between two windows can produce a surge. Sliding window log enforces a limit over a moving interval by storing timestamps.
legacy.rate.tokenLesson: {label} separate burst capacity from the sustained rate.
legacy.rate.fixedLesson: {label} suitable when a quota per calendar interval is your actual goal.
legacy.rate.slidingLesson: {label} stricter, with memory costs proportional to recorded requests.
legacy.rate.distributedLesson: This lab uses one atomic counter. Multiple instances must coordinate counters and time. A non-atomic token check followed by subtraction can allow too many requests through. Explore the implementation in {link}.
legacy.hash.lessonIntro: With modulo, the server count is part of the destination calculation. When it changes, many keys change owners. With consistent hashing, key and node positions remain on the ring; membership changes affect only some ownership intervals.
legacy.hash.virtualLesson: {label} one physical node has several ring positions. Distribution tends to become more balanced with enough points.
legacy.hash.tradeoffLesson: {label} more virtual nodes increase metadata and movement complexity.
legacy.hash.limitsLesson: {label} hashing does not automatically provide replication, durability, or protection against hot keys.
legacy.hash.readingLesson: The lab uses a deterministic 32-bit hash to map 120 keys. There is no production data or network migration. See how virtual nodes are used in {link}.
